title: Price survives match darts to reach Grand Slam semis
content: Gerwyn Price secured a place in the Grand Slam of Darts semifinals after surviving two match darts in a thrilling quarter-final victory over Nico Springer. In the same round, Jermaine Wattimena, who had previously defeated Luke Littler, was eliminated from the tournament.
summary: Gerwyn Price faced two match darts before winning a thrilling quarter‑final against Nico Springer at the Grand Slam of Darts. Luke Littler's conqueror Jermaine Wattimena was knocked out.
author: BBC Sport

title: Man Utd manager hiring and firing costs near £100m
content: Manchester United’s recent managerial turnover has brought the total cost close to £100m. The club borrowed £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach. This appointment incurs a £7.5m compensation payment to US Soccer.
summary: Manchester United borrowed £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach. The club will pay £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer for the appointment.
author: BBC Sport

title: Metastatic pancreatic cancer shows tumor shrinkage with daraxonrasib plus chemotherapy
content: A Phase I/II clinical trial found that combining daraxonrasib with chemotherapy produced substantial tumor shrinkage in patients whose pancreatic cancer had metastasized. The study reported significant responses in these metastatic pancreatic cancer patients.
summary: Daraxonrasib combined with chemotherapy caused substantial tumor shrinkage in patients with pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body. The findings were reported in new results from a Phase I/II clinical trial.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study: Flu vaccine often less effective than advertised
content: Researchers from the University of Maryland report that the annual influenza vaccine is frequently less effective than the 40% to 60% protection rate commonly cited by health officials. Despite this discrepancy, the study’s authors advise that individuals should not skip getting the flu shot.
summary: Researchers from the University of Maryland found that the influenza vaccine is often less protective than the 40% to 60% effectiveness routinely stated by health officials. The study suggests officials may be overselling the vaccine's protective power, though researchers advise people not to skip the shot.
author: Medical Xpress

title: ERAS-0015 'Pan-RAS molecular glue' shows safety and tumor shrinkage in lung and pancreatic cancers
content: Results from the AURORAS-1 Phase I clinical trial indicate that ERAS-0015, a "Pan-RAS molecular glue" anticancer drug, is safe and effective. The study observed tumor shrinkage in patients with difficult-to-treat conditions, specifically lung and pancreatic cancers.
summary: Results from the AURORAS-1 Phase I clinical trial indicate that the anticancer drug ERAS-0015 is safe. The treatment caused tumors to shrink in hard-to-treat diseases such as lung and pancreatic cancer.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Researcher urges reservoir-style safety oversight for hazardous glacial lakes
content: A researcher states that hazardous glacial lakes require reservoir-style safety oversight. As global temperatures rise, thousands of these lakes are expanding behind potentially unstable natural dams. Although these waters pose a flooding risk to downstream communities, they currently lack formal safety regulation.
summary: A researcher states that thousands of glacial lakes behind unstable natural dams are growing as the climate warms. These lakes remain outside formal safety regulation despite the potential risk of flooding to downstream communities.
author: Phys.org

title: A million tiny crystals reveal how semiconductors form distinct cores and shells
content: Perovskites and related perovskitoids are promising semiconductor materials for solar cells, LEDs, and light detectors, with their light absorption and emission properties determined by their ingredients and internal crystal structures. A chip measuring just 2 centimeters across can hold approximately one million tiny crystals, functioning as a miniature material library. This setup reveals how specific mixtures separate into distinct cores and shells, a process that alters the light absorbed by the materials.
summary: Perovskites and perovskitoids are promising semiconductor materials for solar cells, LEDs, and light detectors. A 2-centimeter chip holding roughly a million crystals acts as a miniature library showing how mixtures separate into cores and shells to alter light absorption.
author: Phys.org

title: Study: Following Instagram Profile for 3 Days Reduces Prejudice
content: A research team at the University of Potsdam conducted a field experiment to examine if social media contact can reduce prejudice. The study found that following an unfamiliar Instagram profile for just three days can lead to more favorable attitudes, extending beyond the specific group represented by that profile. These findings were published in the Journal of the Association for Information Systems.
summary: A University of Potsdam field experiment found that following an unfamiliar Instagram profile for three days leads to more favorable attitudes. The study was published in the Journal of the Association for Information Systems.
author: Phys.org

title: Penn State AI model detects crop stress with fewer computations
content: Researchers at Penn State have developed a new artificial intelligence (AI) model capable of detecting stress in agricultural crops using a nondestructive imaging technique. This approach allows for the continuous monitoring of crop health changes over time. The model demonstrates potential for accurately identifying stress resulting from drought, disease, nutrient deficiency, and other factors. Furthermore, it utilizes less computing power than certain existing AI methods, offering a more efficient solution for agricultural analysis.
summary: A new AI model developed by Penn State researchers uses nondestructive imaging to detect crop stress caused by drought, disease, or nutrient deficiency. The model allows for monitoring crop health over time while using less computing power than some existing AI methods.
author: Phys.org

title: Engineer cautions against calling bleach forever chemicals
content: Inside the disinfection room of Baltimore’s Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students in hard hats observed six large vats of bleach. The vats treat water coming from the distant Liberty Reservoir, killing bacteria and other pathogens before the water is sent to the region’s kitchen sinks.
summary: In Baltimore's Ashburton water filtration plant, 14 University of Maryland students in hard hats watched six large vats of bleach treat water from the Liberty Reservoir. The bleach kills bacteria and other pathogens before the water is sent to the region's kitchen sinks.
author: Phys.org

title: Broadening the role of RNA: A messenger, a mediator and now a condensate coordinator
content:
New research into condensates—cellular compartments that serve as hubs for biological reactions—continues to uncover how cells function. The latest studies highlight the expanding roles of these structures, adding to the growing understanding of their importance in cellular biology.

Members of the Marine Biological Laboratory’s condensate consortium are driving this progress. Among them are Amy Gladfelter, a professor at Duke University and current co‑director of the MBL physiology course, and Dragomir Milovanovic, a professor at the Charité Berlin University Institute of Biochemistry. Both scientists have previously been involved with MBL, with Milovanovic having been a former physiology course student and past Whitman fellow.
summary: New research on cellular condensates reveals novel insights into how cells function. The Marine Biological Laboratory's condensate consortium includes Duke University professor Amy Gladfelter, co‑director of the MBL physiology course, and Charité Berlin University Institute of Biochemistry professor Dragomir Milovanovic, a former MBL physiology course student and past Whitman fellow.
author: Phys.org

title: Two new armored tardigrades described from Atlantic seamount
content:
An international research team led by scientists from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven has described two new species of armored marine tardigrades. These tiny organisms were identified in sediment samples collected from the Senghor Seamount located off the coast of Cape Verde. The researchers noted that this discovery highlights the significance of undersea mountains as biodiversity oases.

The study, which provides comprehensive taxonomic descriptions of the newly identified species, has been published in the scientific journal "ZooKeys."
summary: An international team led by researchers from Senckenberg am Meer in Wilhelmshaven described two new species of marine tardigrades. The species were found in the sediment of the Senghor Seamount off Cape Verde and the study, published in ZooKeys, highlights undersea mountains as biodiversity oases.
author: Phys.org

title: Quantum software matches classical benchmark for molecular interaction modeling
content:
Quantum software has recently matched a classical benchmark for a specific molecular interaction, demonstrating that quantum‑based calculations can achieve the same accuracy as traditional methods in this instance.  

Accurate predictions of how molecules interact are essential for drug discovery, providing insights into a drug’s effectiveness, potential side effects, and other pharmacological properties. Computational modeling can reduce the need for costly laboratory experiments, although some interactions still lie beyond the reach of classical computers.
summary: Quantum software has matched the classical benchmark for modeling a molecular interaction. Predicting how molecules interact is central to drug discovery, offering information on drug action and side effects, and computational modeling can reduce the need for costly lab work, although some interactions still exceed classical computational limits.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists crack decades‑old mystery of barium titanate for faster optical communications
content: Researchers at KAIST and Caltech have precisely measured how barium titanate controls and absorbs light, a property that has puzzled scientists for decades. Their study resolves longstanding uncertainties that have slowed the material’s development for ultra‑fast optical communications. By clarifying the light‑management behavior of barium titanate, the findings could make it easier to build optical devices that transmit information faster while wasting less light.
summary: Researchers at KAIST and Caltech measured how barium titanate controls and absorbs light, resolving uncertainties that had slowed its development. The findings may enable faster optical devices that waste less light.
author: Science Daily

title: Groundbreaking X-ray telescope captures first observations after eight years in space
content: After eight years and 10 billion kilometres in space, a groundbreaking X‑ray telescope en route to Mercury has captured its first cosmic observations and is performing better than scientists expected. The instrument may soon uncover Mercury’s hidden chemical secrets and reshape our understanding of how the solar system’s smallest planet formed.
summary: The X‑ray telescope, after eight years and 10 billion kilometers in space, has captured its first cosmic observations. It is performing better than scientists expected and could soon reveal Mercury's hidden chemical secrets, transforming our understanding of how the planet formed.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists Discover Microplastics Generate Reactive Molecules That Damage Cells
content:
Microplastics may be more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies, scientists have discovered. Tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules that damage cells and tissues.  

This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.
summary: Scientists have found that microplastics interact with water to produce highly reactive molecules that can damage cells and tissues. This chemical activity may explain links between microplastic exposure and serious health problems such as heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.
author: Science Daily

title: Voyager 1 signals take 24 hours as probe reaches 16.1 billion miles
content: NASA’s Voyager 1 has traveled 16.1 billion miles from Earth, becoming the first spacecraft whose signals take a full day to reach us. Nearly 50 years after launch, the aging probe remains in interstellar space, continuing its historic journey despite dwindling power and technical challenges.
summary: Voyager 1 is now 16.1 billion miles from Earth, making its signals take a full day to travel back. The probe, launched nearly 50 years ago, continues its journey through interstellar space despite dwindling power and technical challenges.
author: Science Daily

title: Curiosity Captures Drifting Twilight Clouds on Mars
content:
NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover captured images of drifting twilight clouds on October 31, 2026, marking the 5,061st sol of its mission. These post-sunset clouds, which appear briefly each fall over Gale Crater, were observed using the rover’s navigation cameras. The rover has been exploring the crater for more than 14 years.

Curiosity was built by NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. JPL leads the mission on behalf of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate as part of the agency’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio.
summary: NASA’s Curiosity rover photographed drifting twilight clouds on Oct. 31, 2026, the 5,061st sol of the mission. The images were taken with its navigation cameras over Gale Crater, where the rover has been exploring for more than 14 years.
author: NASA News

title: Police departments promote Grand Theft Auto 6 despite game’s contempt for law enforcement
content: Police departments are reportedly using the blockbuster video game Grand Theft Auto 6 as a tool to recruit new members and to admonish the public, even though the game openly displays contempt for law enforcement. The agencies appear unaware of the contrast between the game’s tone and their own messaging.
summary: Grand Theft Auto 6 openly displays contempt for law enforcement. Some police departments are using the game to recruit new members and to scold the public.
author: Wired

title: Boys Noize cites club inspiration for new album 7LLVSION
content:
Boys Noize, the stage name of Alex Ridha, says his recent collaboration with Nine Inch Nails did not shape his forthcoming album 7LLVSION. In an interview with The Verge, Ridha explained that most tracks on the record had already existed for some time and were not designed as rock songs for live shows. Instead, they are “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets.  

Ridha described his creative routine as returning to his usual workflow: he starts by making coffee, then goes into his room and turns on his machines to produce the music. This process, he notes, is what he has always done when crafting club‑ready material.  

The album’s focus, according to Ridha, remains on club-oriented sounds rather than the influence of the Nine Inch Nails production team.
summary: Alex Ridha (Boys Noize) says the Nine Inch Nails collaboration did not influence his new record 7LLVSION. The songs were already developed and are designed for club play and DJ sets rather than live rock performances.
author: The Verge

title: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims to have solved the Riemann hypothesis with Claude
content:
Anthropic went public on November 19, 2026, and shortly after its mathematician Levent Alpöge announced that he had proved the Riemann hypothesis with the help of Claude.  Alpöge said his solution, which would resolve a problem that has stumped mathematicians for decades, has not yet been verified independently.

Anthropic has not commented on or taken part in Alpöge’s claim.  In a document posted on his website, Alpöge noted that he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the breakthrough.
summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims to have proved the Riemann hypothesis using Claude. His solution has not yet been independently verified and Anthropic has not commented on the announcement.
author: The Verge

title: Valve may raise Steam Machine prices due to supply constraints
content: When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn't secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change. "We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels," Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained." If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year. Read full article Comments
summary: Valve says it may need to raise Steam Machine prices because memory and storage costs are rising. The company notes that the 2TB model is especially constrained and the exact price is uncertain.
author: Ars Technica

title: Army Delays Detonation of 68 Lead Azide Barrels After Court Stay
content:
The U.S. Army announced on Thursday that it would postpone a plan to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an installation in Middletown, Iowa. The barrels, stored in earth‑covered concrete containment structures, were scheduled for two simultaneous controlled detonations around noon on Friday. The Army had warned that the explosions could release toxic gas and lead, potentially dispersing a plume of neurotoxic lead up to 100 miles north of the site, according to modeling released earlier that week.

A federal appeals court issued an emergency order later on Thursday that halted the planned detonations. In response, the Army rescheduled the blast for November 23 to allow more time to communicate with residents of Iowa, many of whom had not been aware of the planned detonations until this week.

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said on social media that public communication is essential to public trust. He added that the Army would continue to engage with state and local officials to provide accurate, up‑to‑date information about the situation.
summary: In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order.
author: Ars Technica

title: Okunoshima Island in Japan: hundreds of rabbits and a secret chemical weapons past
content:
Hundreds of rabbits roam freely on Japan’s Okunoshima Island, delighting visitors from around the world.  
Beneath its idyllic scenery, the island has a troubling history of secret chemical weapons production.
summary: Hundreds of rabbits roam freely on Japan's Okunoshima Island, attracting visitors worldwide. The island also has a history of secret chemical weapons production.
author: Euronews

title: Protesters rally outside Anthropic HQ demanding AI regulation after $2 trillion IPO
content: Protesters gathered outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters on 19 November 2026 to demand tighter regulation and greater human control over artificial intelligence. The demonstration followed the company’s $2 trillion stock‑market debut.
summary: Protesters gathered outside Anthropic’s San Francisco headquarters on 19 November 2026. They demanded tighter regulation and greater human control over artificial intelligence following the company’s $2 trillion stock market debut.
author: Euronews

title: Around 20 isolated Awá Indigenous people approach Brazilian government outpost seeking yams
content: A video captured around 20 members of Brazil’s isolated Awá Indigenous group approaching a government outpost in the Amazon. The group requested yams before returning to the forest. The encounter, described as rare, has prompted concerns about the Awá’s health and potential food shortages.
summary: Around 20 members of Brazil’s isolated Awá Indigenous group approached a government outpost in the Amazon and asked for yams before returning to the forest. The rare encounter has raised concerns about their health and possible food shortages.
author: Euronews

title: Iran prepares convoy of over 14 tankers at Kharg Island to test US oil blockade
content: Iran has positioned more than 14 tankers at Kharg Island, the terminal that handles up to 90 % of the country’s crude exports, according to satellite imagery and ship‑tracking data. The crewed, Iranian‑flagged vessels are set to form a convoy heading toward the Sea of Oman in the coming days, a move described as a test of the U.S. oil blockade.
summary: More than 14 tankers have been assigned crews and Iranian flags at the terminal that handles up to 90% of the country’s crude exports, according to satellite imagery and ship‑tracking data. The convoy is expected to head toward the Sea of Oman in the coming days.
author: Euronews

title: Bhutan's Shing Tshon wood painting preserves architectural tradition
content: Bhutan’s artisans hand‑paint intricate patterns on wooden buildings, preserving a centuries‑old tradition known as Shing Tshon. The craft remains central to the kingdom’s cultural identity.
summary: In Bhutan, artisans hand‑paint intricate patterns on wooden buildings, preserving a centuries‑old tradition. The craft, called Shing Tshon, remains central to the kingdom’s cultural identity.
author: Euronews

title: Thousands of Berlin students march against rearmament and compulsory service
content: On Friday, 20 November 2026, thousands of students marched through Berlin to protest Germany’s rapid military rearmament and fears of a return to compulsory military service. The demonstration was part of a broader wave of youth protests across Europe.
summary: Thousands of students marched through Berlin on Friday 20 November 2026, protesting the country's rapid military rearmament and fears of a return to compulsory military service. The demonstration was part of a broader wave of youth protests across Europe.
author: Euronews

title: Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine, missiles hit Poland
content: Moscow launched massive strikes on Ukraine on Friday, and Kyiv reported that at least six people were killed in the Ukrainian capital. Poland said two Russian missiles likely landed in its south‑east corner, calling the incident a “provocation” by Moscow. Earlier in the day, Russian President Vladimir Putin promised a “painful” response to Kyiv’s strikes on the Crimea bridge after a summit that included China’s Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump. The report comes from France 24’s Gulliver Cragg in Kyiv.
summary: Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine, missiles hit Poland.
author: France 24

title: Burnham calls EU-UK trade, emissions and youth deal a landmark “good day”
content:
Britain and the European Union announced on Friday that they have reached agreements covering trade, carbon emissions and youth mobility, and they pledged to rebuild ties through an “ambitious and dynamic” post‑Brexit relationship. In a joint statement issued after a summit in Brussels, the parties said the deals will eliminate checks on the trade of plant and animal products, link their emissions‑trading schemes and allow 100,000 young adults from each side to live and work in the other’s country for up to three years.

British minister Burnham described the outcome as a “landmark” EU‑UK deal and called it a “good day” for Britain and Europe. France 24’s International Affairs Editor Kethevane Gorjestani provided further commentary.
summary: Burnham calls EU-UK trade, emissions and youth deal a landmark “good day”.
author: France 24

title: Blade Runner 2099 and Rivals highlighted as top TV releases this month
content: "Blade Runner" returns with a futuristic twist, while British bonkbuster "Rivals" is back with part two of season two. TV critic Dheepthika Laurent joins Eve Jackson to review the month’s big releases, including Netflix’s acclaimed Arctic comedy "North of North" and the lavish K-drama "Remarried Empress".
summary: Blade Runner returns with a futuristic twist, and British bonkbuster Rivals is back with part two of season two. TV critic Dheepthika Laurent joins Eve Jackson to review Netflix’s Arctic comedy North of North and the K‑drama Remarried Empress.
author: France 24

title: French police investigate Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq over alleged 2018 gang rape
content: French police are investigating allegations that actor Gérard Depardieu, a convicted sex offender, raped and assaulted a woman with the complicity of bestselling author Michel Houellebecq during a 2018 film shoot, two sources said on Friday. The plaintiff has also accused the film’s director, Guillaume Nicloux, of being complicit in the abuse.
summary: French police are investigating allegations that actor Gérard Depardieu raped and assaulted a woman with the complicity of author Michel Houellebecq during a 2018 film shoot. The plaintiff also accuses director Guillaume Nicloux of being complicit in the abuse.
author: France 24

title: Photography originated in France, exploring its legacy
content: Photography, now a ubiquitous tool for creative expression and everyday documentation, originated in France. FRANCE 24’s Tanishk Saha examines this French legacy, highlighting the country’s role in developing the technology that made photography an essential, widely‑accessible medium since its invention.
summary: Photography has become an essential and widely-accessible medium since its invention. The technology was developed in France and FRANCE 24's Tanishk Saha examines its French legacy.
author: France 24

title: Trump calls relationships with Xi and Putin “fantastic” after first trilateral talks
content: U.S. President Donald Trump described his relationships with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin as “fantastic” during a White House press conference on Friday. He made the remarks after returning to Washington from a first‑ever trilateral meeting with the Chinese and Russian leaders.
summary: US President Donald Trump said his relationships with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin are “fantastic” during a White House press conference on Friday. The comments followed his return to Washington after a first‑ever trilateral meeting with the Chinese and Russian leaders.
author: France 24

title: Tom Standage on America’s “Donroe Doctrine” in The World Ahead 2027
content: The Economist's deputy editor Tom Standage joins us for a futuristic retrospective, taking us back to the future as we spotlight "The World Ahead 2027". We begin with the "leader of the free world", the FIFA Peace Prize recipient presiding over an America under the "Donroe Doctrine": "Its enemies no longer fear it and its allies no longer trust it in the way they did before."
summary: Tom Standage on America’s “Donroe Doctrine” in The World Ahead 2027.
author: France 24

title: Bangladesh protests turn violent with bomb blasts, arson ahead of Hasina's planned return
content:
The Awami League announced a nationwide protest on Thursday after the government denied former prime minister Sheikh Hasina’s request for a passport. The party had earlier outlined a week‑long programme of rallies and protests to build support for Hasina’s planned return in December, ending with a nationwide lockdown on Thursday.

Supporters of Hasina’s movement triggered violent protests across parts of Bangladesh, shutting down areas and sparking clashes, bomb blasts and arson attacks. The unrest included the burning of the ancestral home of former leader Muhammad Yunus, and the title reports that killings accompanied the violence.
summary: Awami League called for a week‑long programme of protests and a nationwide lockdown on Thursday after the government rejected Sheikh Hasina’s passport request. Thursday protests in parts of Bangladesh sparked clashes, bomb blasts, arson attacks and the ancestral home of former leader Muhammad Yunus was set ablaze.
author: Guardian World

title: UN top court rules Myanmar military committed genocide against Rohingya
content:
Tears fell in the halls of The Hague as the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar’s 2017 campaign against the Rohingya constituted genocide. The decision, announced at the UN’s top court, was met with an eruption of applause in refugee camps across Bangladesh, where the scattered Rohingya community gathered to witness the verdict.

The ruling confirms that the Myanmar military intentionally sought to destroy the mostly Muslim minority through mass killings and rape. The court’s judgment follows nearly a decade of waiting by the Rohingya, who have suffered the loss of more than 10,000 lives and the displacement of about 700,000 people to neighbouring Bangladesh. The next steps, the court noted, will depend on governments worldwide.
summary: The UN’s top court ruled that the Myanmar military had committed genocide against the Rohingya. The verdict sparked tears in The Hague and applause in Bangladesh refugee camps, after more than 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 700,000 fled to Bangladesh.
author: Guardian World

title: US cautious on ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling as EU lauds court's critical role
content:
The United States greeted the International Court of Justice’s Thursday ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority with caution, while the European Union praised what it called a “critical” role for the UN’s top court. China, in contrast, voiced concerns that the decision represented judicial overreach.

The historic ruling marks the first time the ICJ has found a state responsible for genocide, a judgment that observers say could establish a precedent for future genocide claims, including a pending case against Israel. Reactions to the decision highlighted deep international divisions over the court’s authority and the broader role of similar institutions.
summary: US cautious on ICJ Myanmar genocide ruling as EU lauds court's critical role.
author: Guardian World

title: Indian man Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 19 years for plot to kill Sikh separatist in NYC
content:
Indian businessman Nikhil Gupta, 55, was sentenced to more than 19 years in a U.S. prison on Friday after admitting he plotted with an Indian government official to hire a hitman to kill a Sikh separatist in New York City. The victim, a dual U.S.–Canadian citizen, was targeted as part of a broader effort to silence Indian dissidents, according to U.S. and Canadian authorities.

Gupta pleaded guilty in February to three charges: murder‑for‑hire, conspiracy to commit murder‑for‑hire, and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The court found that his plan was backed by the Indian government, but the hitman’s attempt failed, leading to the sentencing.
summary: Indian man Nikhil Gupta sentenced to 19 years for plot to kill Sikh separatist in NYC.
author: Guardian World

title: NSW passes law to boost Mount Pleasant coal output, Greens say it targets One Nation
content: Labor says allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’ Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation. After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.
summary: NSW passes law to boost Mount Pleasant coal output, Greens say it targets One Nation.
author: Guardian World

title: Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last
content:
The Victorian Greens have filed an urgent application with the Supreme Court seeking an injunction to halt the distribution of how‑to‑vote cards by independent candidate Tosh‑Jake Finnigan. The Greens allege the cards copy the party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo and display the banner “Vote 1 Green Values” while directing voters to preference the Greens last.

According to the filing, the cards also instruct voters in a manner that would benefit the Liberal Party. The Greens contend the material misuses their branding and misleads voters, prompting the legal challenge as pre‑polling began on Wednesday morning.
summary: Victorian Greens seek urgent injunction over how-to-vote cards mimicking party’s branding but preferencing it last.
author: Guardian World

title: Mamdani announces plan to close Rikers Island jail by 2032
content: Mamdani announced a plan to close New York’s Rikers Island jail by 2032. The effort builds on proposals that began in 2019, when the city council voted to shut the facility but encountered delays over where to house its inmates.
summary: Mamdani announced a plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by 2032. Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it but delays arose over where to place inmates.
author: BBC World

title: Japan's Hayabusa Makes First Spacecraft Liftoff From Asteroid Itokawa
content:
On November 19, 2005, Japan’s Hayabusa spacecraft achieved the first-ever liftoff from the surface of an asteroid. The mission, operated by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA), was primarily designed to collect samples from asteroid Itokawa and return them to Earth. Although the primary goal was sample collection rather than demonstrating a liftoff capability, the event marked a significant milestone in space exploration. Hayabusa had originally launched on May 9, 2003, but its arrival at the asteroid was delayed until September 2005 after a solar storm degraded its solar arrays and limited power for its ion engines.

Despite these challenges, Hayabusa reached Itokawa on September 12, 2005. During its first landing attempt on November 19, the spacecraft descended to a point just 56 feet above the surface before going silent for three hours. Once contact was restored, JAXA officials confirmed the probe had landed. According to Andrew Cheng, a Hayabusa science team member at Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory, the spacecraft bounced off the surface several times and rested on the asteroid for approximately 39 minutes. However, the samplers did not fire during this initial touchdown.

Following the first landing, Hayabusa lifted off for a second attempt, which occurred on November 26, 2005. Controllers remained uncertain whether any material had been gathered during these events, so they proceeded to send the spacecraft back to Earth anyway. The sample return capsule eventually touched down in Australia in June 2010. In November 2010, JAXA announced that scientists had found 1,500 dust grains from Itokawa inside the capsule. These samples were confirmed to have been jammed into the collector by the two landings, despite the collector mechanism failing to fire.

The success of the Hayabusa mission spurred the creation of a follow-up sample-return mission called Hayabusa2. That probe launched in December 2014 and arrived at asteroid Ryugu in 2018. Hayabusa2 successfully collected its own samples and returned them to Earth in December 2020. Currently, the Hayabusa2 probe is on an extended mission to the asteroid 2015 BM510, which it will fly by in April 2028. A planned landing on the asteroid 1998 KY26 became impossible due to engine trouble.
summary: On Nov. 19, 2005, the Japanese Hayabusa spacecraft achieved the first-ever liftoff from an asteroid surface during its mission to collect samples from Itokawa. Although the sampling mechanism did not fire, scientists later confirmed the capsule returned 1,500 dust grains to Earth in 2010.
author: Space.com

title: Could an ancient solar eclipse rewrite Egyptian history?
content:
The solar system functions as a precise celestial clock that can be projected both into the future and the past. On August 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse will sweep across Egypt, with the moon’s shadow passing directly over Luxor. According to Time and Date, totality in Luxor will begin at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last for 6 minutes and 22 seconds. While astronomers can calculate these events centuries in advance, the same calculations allow them to reconstruct where eclipses occurred thousands of years ago. When ancient texts reliably describe such events, they provide precise timestamps to anchor historical moments to specific places and times.

Astronomical calculations indicate that a total solar eclipse crossed northern Egypt on April 1, 2471 B.C., during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that this event may explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf departed from tradition to build a large rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. However, this remains a hypothesis because no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse, and using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that contemporaries observed and documented the event.

A more intriguing possibility involves an annular solar eclipse that occurred over Canaan on October 30, 1207 B.C. Researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. published research in 2017 suggesting this event is described in the Old Testament book of Joshua. The biblical passage recounts Joshua praying for the sun and moon to stand still while the Israelites fought their enemies in Gibeon and the Valley of Aijalon. If this interpretation is correct, it would represent the oldest recorded solar eclipse with an identified date.

This potential identification has significant implications for Egyptian chronology, specifically regarding the reign of Pharaoh Ramesses II, who ruled for 66 years during the New Kingdom and commissioned major structures such as Abu Simbel and additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple. While historians generally date the reign of his successor, Pharaoh Merneptah, to approximately 1213–1203 B.C., the precise dates of Ramesses II’s rule remain subject to debate. Humphreys and Waddington proposed that the 1207 B.C. eclipse occurred during the second, third, or fourth year of Merneptah’s reign, which would refine the conventional dates for Ramesses II’s rule from 1279–1213 B.C. to approximately 1276–1210 B.C.

The interpretation of the biblical text remains controversial. Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs has challenged the eclipse theory, arguing that the narrative describes the sun over Gibeon and the moon over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously, which is inconsistent with an eclipse. Despite the ambiguity surrounding the 1207 B.C. event, the celestial mechanics that predict the upcoming 2027 eclipse are the same forces that allow researchers to analyze ancient skies. While the 2027 event is certain, the 1207 B.C. eclipse serves as a potential, though debated, timestamp that could help clarify the timeline of ancient Egyptian imperial power.

title: NASA Perseverance and Odyssey halt science work due to antenna and wheel glitches
content:
NASA announced on Thursday, Nov. 19, that two of its Mars explorers, the Perseverance rover and the Mars Odyssey orbiter, have suspended science operations due to technical glitches. The agency expects both spacecraft to resume work by the end of November. Perseverance is dealing with an antenna issue, while the Odyssey orbiter is experiencing problems with a reaction wheel.

Perseverance, which landed in Jezero Crater in February 2021, has recently set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, surpassing the previous record held by the Opportunity rover on Oct. 11. However, 19 days later, the mission team identified a problem where the rover’s main UHF downlink radio failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer. The rover autonomously switched to its backup UHF radio and entered a protective "safe mode," shutting down non-essential systems. Although the team recovered the rover from safe mode, they discovered the backup radio was transmitting at approximately half of its expected power output. Consequently, handlers have stopped using the backup radio, and Perseverance is now communicating directly with Earth via its high-gain antenna and NASA’s Deep Space Network. This direct pathway offers lower data rates, prompting the team to pause science work, including camera observations, to prioritize diagnostic information. NASA officials stated that the rover is stable and communicating with the team.

The Mars Odyssey orbiter, which arrived at Mars in October 2001, recently lost the use of one of its four reaction wheels, which are essential for maintaining orientation in space. The issue began on Nov. 4 when the orbiter entered safe mode, a state it remained in until Nov. 6 while the team diagnosed the problem. Mission members have made some progress, including getting the faulty wheel to move when commanded, but further testing is required to confirm if the wheel is recoverable. Although Odyssey has been out of safe mode for two weeks, it has not yet resumed its science or data-relay operations. The goal is for the orbiter to return to full operations during the last week of November.

If the reaction wheel cannot be recovered, the mission team will have to orient the orbiter solely using its thrusters. According to NASA, Odyssey has enough hydrazine fuel left to perform this maneuver for only one or two months. Despite this potential limitation, the orbiter has operated at Mars longer than any other spacecraft and has made significant scientific contributions. These include creating the first global maps detailing the composition of the Martian surface, identifying hazards at landing sites, spotting locations of scientific interest for other missions, and mapping water molecules in the top three feet of the surface, including buried ice that could be useful for future astronauts.
summary: NASA's Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have paused science operations due to an antenna issue and a faulty reaction wheel, respectively. NASA aims to have both spacecraft resume work by the end of November, though Odyssey's mission duration is limited if the wheel is not recoverable.

title: Don't turn the moon into the Wild West, scientists warn
content:
Researchers are urging for a temporary ban on the industrial exploitation of the moon to prevent irreversible environmental damage and the destruction of scientific resources. This call comes as both China and the United States advance plans to establish permanent human settlements on the lunar surface by the end of the next decade. Commercial entities are also preparing to support these efforts by mining resources such as water, construction materials, industrial metals, and rare earth minerals.

Florian Rabitz, a professor of climate and technology governance at Vilnius University in Lithuania, and Xiao-Shan Yap, an assistant professor of Earth-space sustainability at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, published an article in the journal Global Environmental Politics last month. They advocate for "robust international regulations" and "broad and inclusive deliberation" to ensure the global community can carefully assess the economic impacts on the moon. The researchers argue that a moratorium is necessary to allow regulatory frameworks to develop before a "moon rush" compromises the pristine lunar environment.

Beyond environmental concerns, the pair object to the potential colonization of the moon by a limited group of powerful nations, specifically China, the U.S., and their close allies. Rabitz stated that nations undertaking major infrastructure projects will likely assert their positions by defining exclusive territories, a scenario he described as unacceptable. Although the United Nations' 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits individual nations from appropriating the moon, Rabitz noted that the lunar body is unlikely to remain neutral if its exploitation is driven by a small number of dominant powers.
summary: Researchers are calling for a moratorium on industrial exploitation of the moon, fearing that rapid development could cause irreversible environmental damage and destroy invaluable scientific material. Both China and the U.

title: On this day in space! Nov. 20, 1998:  Russia launches 1st module of International Space Station as construction begins on the largest human-built structure in orbit
content:
On November 20, 1998, the first module of the International Space Station, named Zarya, launched into orbit atop a Russian Proton rocket. Weighing 42,600 pounds and measuring approximately 41 feet in length and 13.5 feet in width, the module is comparable in size to a tour bus. Zarya, also known as the Functional Cargo Block or FGB, served as the core module around which the rest of the station was constructed. Although built by the Russians, the module was funded by the United States, with NASA paying $220 million for its construction at the Krunichev State Research and Production Space Center in Moscow.

The decision to contract a Russian company for the build was driven by cost efficiency, as the price was half of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. Work on Zarya began in 1994 and concluded in 1998. The module is designed as a central hub based on the success of Russia's Salyut space station designs, featuring two solar arrays for power and 16 external tanks for propellant storage. It also includes docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft, which transport crews to and from the station.

Two weeks after Zarya’s launch, NASA’s STS-88 shuttle mission aboard the space shuttle Endeavour brought the Unity module into space. The astronauts on STS-88 connected the two modules in orbit, marking the initial assembly of the station. While Zarya and Unity formed the initial structure, the station was not large enough to accommodate a permanent crew until Russia’s Zvezda service module launched in 2000 and docked with Zarya’s aft section. This expansion allowed the station to host its first three-person crew, Expedition 1, in 2000.

Today, the International Space Station is approximately the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. Over the last 28 years, the station has been expanded with giant backbone-like metal trusses, solar wings, and numerous other modules built by Russia, NASA, Europe, Canada, and Japan. Zarya is now primarily used for storage and as a housing for external fuel tanks. Many ISS components could not be tested together on the ground, meaning their first attachment occurred in space during the construction process.

The International Space Station has maintained steady rotating crews of astronauts since the year 2000. As of the time of writing, the station is 28 years old. The continuous presence of crews and the expansion of the structure represent a significant feat of space engineering, with China’s Tiangong space station recently emerging as a rival in orbital construction.
summary: On Nov. 20, 1998, the first piece of the International Space Station launched into orbit.

title: Ben Dark's Green Kingdom review: A gardener explores plant dynasties and natural history
content: A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous prose John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal. Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. He is a professional gardener, yet his tastes run to the surprisingly sludgy. Orchids and roses have their place in the Green Kingdom, but nothing thrills him more than an evil-looking pond, rich in microscopic nutrients.
summary: Ben Dark, a professional gardener, traces the evolution of plant dynasties in his book Green Kingdom, ranging from pond scum to alpine meadows. The review highlights Dark's focus on the sexual aspects of plant life and his preference for microscopic nutrients over traditional ornamental flowers.

title: Japanese researchers identify key cells and pathways in post-thoracic surgery adhesion formation
content:
Intrathoracic adhesions following thoracic surgery can elevate the risk of complications during subsequent procedures, yet the specific molecular mechanisms driving their formation have remained unclear. To address this gap, a Japanese research team published a Letter in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy detailing their efforts to develop an animal model that accurately mimics patient pleural adhesions.

The study focused on identifying the key cells and signaling pathways responsible for adhesion formation. By establishing this model, the researchers aimed to uncover new methods for preventing adhesions after thoracic surgery.

title: NASA Honor Awards Ceremony Recognizes Employees at Stennis Space Center
content:
NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, held its Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18 to recognize employees contributing to the agency’s mission. The awards were presented by Christine Powell, the center director, and Jeremy Parsons, NASA’s Artemis program manager, who is responsible for the management and oversight of the initiative to return humans to the Moon. The event highlighted individual achievements in leadership, engineering, and service, as well as team accomplishments and long-term civil service milestones.

Stephen Rawls of Carriere, Mississippi, received the Center Director’s Excellence Award for exceptional leadership and technical excellence in advancing propulsion testing capabilities for critical NASA and commercial programs. Bradley Tyree, also of Carriere, was honored with the Engineering Excellence Award for his contributions to the successful testing of the Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment Confined by Missile Program. Anna Lizana of Diamondhead, Mississippi, received the Excellence in Customer Service Award for environmental compliance support that advanced commercial partnerships and reduced regulatory risk.

Additional individual recipients included Daniel Jones of Huntsville, Alabama, who received the Excellence in Innovation Award for inventing a system for low-cost aerodynamic data acquisition known as the Hydrocarbon Propellants Enabling Reproduction of Flows in Rocket Engines. Peyton Pinson of Carriere was awarded the Leadership Excellence Award for his role as E-1 test director, while Joseph Schuyler of Pass Christian received the J. Harry Guin Leadership Award for advancing the center’s propulsion testing capability. Michael McDaniel of Slidell, Louisiana, received the Roy S. Estess Service Leadership Award for his partnership and commitment to the community as the general manager of L3Harris Technologies at NASA Stennis.

The Space Flight Awareness Trailblazer Award was presented to Amer Arshad of Diamondhead and Claire O’Shaughnessy of Mandeville, Louisiana, for innovative leadership and collaborative efforts that strengthened the center’s mission and advanced critical facility capabilities for the Artemis program. The Liquid Oxygen/Liquid Methane Assessment, Confined by Missile Test Team also received the Space Flight Awareness Team Award for executing a test series that provided mission-critical safety data for human spaceflight. Briou Bourgeois accepted the team award on behalf of a group that included Chase Aubry, Brandon Carver, and numerous other staff members.

The ceremony also recognized employees who reached significant anniversary milestones in their civil service careers. Those with 40 years of service included Curtis Armstrong, Jason Edge, and Kevin Power. Employees with 35 years of service were Michael Brashear, Reginald Ellis II, Arlen Griffey, Bradley Messer, Christine Powell, and Michael Rewis. Skip Roberts was recognized for 30 years of service, while a group of 15 employees, including Gregory Carmouche, Thomas Carroll, and Joseph Schuyler, were honored for 25 years of service.
summary: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) Stephen Rawls, second from right with guest, receives the Center Director’s Excellence Award during the Honor Awards ceremony on Nov. 18 at NASA’s Stennis Space Center.

title: OpenComputer offers open source cloud coding agent with 24‑second commit speed
content:
Utpal, one of the founders of OpenComputer, announced the project on Hacker News. OpenComputer is an open‑source cloud coding agent designed for teams that can run directly in a user’s own cloud account, including AWS, GCP, and Azure. The agent harness and sandbox operate on the same durable virtual machine, as described in the architecture documentation. In benchmark tests, the first commit lands in 24 seconds, while the alternatives Utpal evaluated took between 53 and 72 seconds.

The system is built to scale horizontally with a single VM per team. Sessions are isolated in git worktrees, and session files are backed up to a repository after every turn, allowing any session to resume on another VM. Utpal notes that after roughly 640 session‑hours a month, a single always‑on 4‑vCPU VM becomes cheaper than per‑session E2B sandboxes, making the setup faster and more cost‑efficient than current state‑of‑the‑art coding agents.

OpenComputer is available for a free cloud trial or can be self‑hosted. A full demo is posted on X, and the project welcomes feedback. The Hacker News discussion can be found at the provided comments URL, where the post has earned 31 points and 12 comments.
summary: OpenComputer is an open source cloud coding agent that runs on a single durable VM in a user’s AWS, GCP or Azure account. Its first commit lands in 24 seconds, faster than the 53‑72 second benchmarked alternatives, and it becomes cheaper than per‑session sandboxes after roughly 640 session‑hours per month.

Ahead of Black Friday, Samsung’s 256GB model is available for $44.99 at Amazon, a discount from its usual price and significantly below its $79.99 MSRP. Sandisk’s 256GB card is also discounted, available for $49.99 from Amazon and Sandisk, which is $10 off Amazon’s typical list price.

For users seeking more capacity, both brands offer 512GB microSD Express cards for $99.99 on Amazon. This provides double the storage for approximately twice the price of the 256GB options. Sandisk’s 512GB card is also listed at Best Buy for $99.99 and on Amazon for $98.99. The article notes that the 256GB option is likely sufficient for most Switch 2 players unless they purchase a large volume of games.

Storage requirements vary significantly by title. For example, the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 24.9 gigabytes, while other Nintendo-developed games tend to have similar install sizes. Third-party titles vary widely; Resident Evil Requiem is relatively small at 28.7 gigabytes, whereas The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered takes up about 50 gigabytes. Some games require even more storage space.
summary: Expanding your Nintendo Switch 2’s 256GB of built-in storage with a microSD card is pricier than it was with Nintendo’s original console. That’s because microSD Express cards, while physically identical to ones you might have lying around, have faster read and write speeds.

title: FCC approves prison jamming tech; CTIA warns of lawful call interference
content:
The Federal Communications Commission approved a proposal that allows state and local prisons to deploy jamming technology to block contraband cellphones. The ruling follows a pilot test that revealed significant issues with the jamming system.

In the pilot, conducted by the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and the South Carolina Department of Corrections, a limited number of micro‑jammers were used. The test showed that the jammers blocked 911 calls, interfered with public‑safety and other communications, and caused interference up to two and a half miles from the devices. Despite restrictions on spectrum bands and power levels, the system still disrupted legitimate communications.

The pilot also found gaps in the jamming coverage. In outdoor inmate recreation areas, the jammers failed to block contraband device calls in one‑half to two‑thirds of attempts. The wireless industry lobby group CTIA reported that the technology appears both over‑inclusive—blocking lawful communications—and under‑inclusive—failing to stop a significant portion of contraband device usage.
summary: FCC approves prison jamming tech; CTIA warns of lawful call interference.

title: SpaceX recovers Starship, clearing hurdle for NASA Moon plans and orbital refuel demo
content:
SpaceX’s successful mid‑air recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend has removed a key obstacle on NASA’s path to the Moon. The operation demonstrated that the company can retrieve a fully fueled vehicle after launch, a capability that could allow for higher launch rates and support a long‑delayed orbital refueling demonstration scheduled for next year.

For SpaceX, the recovery gives engineers a practical test of rapid Starship reuse, which is expected to accelerate the deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA sees a higher cadence of launches as a way to speed learning as SpaceX works on a deep‑space version of Starship that could ferry astronaut crews to the lunar surface.

SpaceX plans to bring a second Starship launch site online at Kennedy Space Center in Florida early next year. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, adding to the company’s existing production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites and factories, SpaceX will have the infrastructure needed to advance its Starship program further.
summary: SpaceX's successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA's path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year. For SpaceX's purposes, Saturday's mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships.
author: Ars Technica

title: Giant star in Andromeda swallows companion, ends in explosion
content:
Astronomers have captured, for the first time, a giant star in the Andromeda Galaxy swallowing its smaller companion over a period of nearly a decade. The event, described in a new study published in Nature, was led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University. The star, about seven times the mass of the Sun, slowly engulfed the smaller star, a process known as common envelope evolution, before ending in an explosive eruption in late 2025.

Karambelkar noted that the entire sequence “lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” emphasizing that such events are brief compared with the millions‑of‑year timescales of stellar evolution. Common envelope evolution explains how some of the Universe’s tightest binary pairs form: when one star expands into a giant, its outer layers can envelop its companion, creating a shared, loosely bound envelope. Friction within this envelope drains orbital energy, causing the stars to spiral inward. Depending on how much of the envelope is lost, the pair may end up in a much tighter orbit or merge entirely.
summary: Giant star in Andromeda swallows companion, ends in explosion.
author: Ars Technica

title: Researcher HD Moore plants 2 million digital canaries in AI routers, uncovers widespread data leaks
content:
Researchers have revealed a significant privacy vulnerability in the AI services ecosystem by planting 2 million digital canaries—secrets that never had been used before—into prompts sent through a wide network of AI services. The experiment, designed to test whether sensitive information can leak through the chain of AI providers, uncovered an ecosystem that leaks highly sensitive data with little resistance.

The study focused on AI “routers” or “gateways,” such as OpenRouter and Vercel, which act as brokers for AI applications. These services receive large numbers of prompts from end‑user apps and route them to an inference engine based on criteria like lowest price or task suitability. Instead of connecting directly to major providers such as Anthropic or OpenAI, developers often rely on these routers to find the most appropriate model.

To test for leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a set of AWS access keys, unused credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, SSH passwords, unique URLs, DNS names, and private Git repository references. Each secret was seeded into a single prompt sent to one provider. If any secret appeared in a response, the canary would reveal the specific link in the chain responsible for the leak.

The findings show that sensitive data can traverse the AI supply chain with minimal protection, exposing developers and users to potential security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations.
summary: HD Moore embedded 2 million unique secret canaries into prompts routed through AI services like OpenRouter and Vercel. The test showed that many AI apps leaked the seeded AWS keys, passwords, URLs and other sensitive data, indicating a broad privacy breach.

title: Meta reconsiders 2030 net-zero goal amid record emissions from AI data centers
content:
Meta executives are re-evaluating the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030, a shift disclosed in the firm’s latest sustainability report. This reconsideration follows a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions, a rise that exceeds that of other major technology competitors building new AI data centers.

In the November 19, 2026, report, Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta, noted that while long-term ambitions remain unchanged, the operating environment has shifted. They attributed this need for reassessment to the fact that demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.

Peterson and Swedeen stated that Meta is re-evaluating its timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones, including the 2030 net-zero timeframe and near-term intensity targets. The goal of this review is to ensure the company’s approach reflects current operating realities while maintaining transparent progress year over year.
summary: Meta’s executives are rethinking the company’s original goal of achieving net-zero emissions by 2030. That revelation in Meta’s latest sustainability report comes as the company reported a record percentage increase in greenhouse gas emissions that exceeds any other Big Tech competitor racing to build new AI data centers.

title: FCC orders California to halt enforcement of COLR rules against AT&T
content:
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has ordered the state of California to cease enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort (COLR) rules against AT T. The decision underscores a continuing conflict between the Trump administration and California over the state’s authority to enforce its own telecommunications regulations.

Under California law, AT T’s status as a Carrier of Last Resort obligates it to provide telephone service to any potential customer within its territory. AT T has requested to stop offering basic phone service to new customers and to discontinue service for 184,000 residential customers and 15,000 business customers effective June 1, 2027.

The FCC’s order, released today, granted AT T’s request to preempt the state rules, following the agency’s earlier approval of AT T’s petition to discontinue service. AT T had previously sought the same outcome through the courts, but a federal judge rejected its request to override California’s rules in July.
summary: The FCC ordered California to stop enforcing its Carrier of Last Resort rules against AT&T. AT&T will discontinue basic phone service for 184,000 residential and 15,000 business customers on June 1, 2027.
