title: Palestinian Artists Display Massacre Memories in Dublin Exhibition
content:
IMMA in Dublin has opened an exhibition that brings together artists from across the Levant to confront their region’s traumatic past. The show features works that record historical atrocities while expressing anger, melancholy, and defiance.

A central piece by Simone Fattal consists of basalt slabs onto which she has painted the names of sites associated with massacres since 1948—Deir Yassin, Jenin, Qana, and Sabra. The names are rendered in Arabic script and run alongside a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.” The basalt, a stone that was once molten lava, underscores the permanence of the memory.

The last massacre listed, Qana, was carried out by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982. It inspired the poem “Praise for the High Shadow” by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which the exhibition takes its title. Darwish, writing in exile in Beirut, used the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, linking people scattered around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland.

Together, the works of these mostly Palestinian artists weave a national history of trauma into the cosmopolitan culture of the Levant and the interconnected world of today.
summary: The Dublin exhibition showcases works by Palestinian artists from the Levant, including Simone Fattal’s basalt slab paintings of massacre sites and Etel Adnan’s poetry. It also features photocollages of bulldozed airports, references Mahmoud Darwish’s poems, and expresses the artists’ anger, melancholy, and defiance while weaving traumatic national history into cosmopolitan Levant culture.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Fincher Directs Tarantino Script for Cliff Booth Sequel Featuring Brad Pitt
content:
The review notes that The Further Mis‑Adventures of Cliff Booth is a 140‑minute film written by Quentin Tarantino and directed by David Fincher, continuing the story from Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. The piece highlights that the film does not address the question of whether Brad Pitt’s stuntman character, Cliff Booth, murdered his wife—a topic that appears only in Tarantino’s novel based on the earlier movie.

According to the review, the sequel focuses on Cliff’s “amiable‑cowpoke” persona, culminating in a dramatic rescue and his refusal of an age‑gap relationship with Margaret Qualley’s jailbait teen. The film is described as a “sugar‑rush sequel” that delivers energy, fun, scabrous black comedy, provocative bad taste, and a distinct filmmaking style, while leaving the subject of Cliff’s matrimonial circumstances untouched until Tarantino’s forthcoming crossover novel.

The reviewer frames the movie as part of a multimedia narrative event, suggesting that the film and the novel together will provide a fuller picture of Cliff Booth’s story.
summary: David Fincher directs Quentin Tarantino’s script for a 140‑minute sequel to Once Upon a Time in Hollywood, starring Brad Pitt as Cliff Booth. The film leaves the question of Cliff’s alleged murder of his wife unresolved and is set to be part of a multimedia narrative with a forthcoming novel.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Pochettino urges United to face Liverpool with no fear
content: New head coach’s first game is at Anfield on Sunday ‘We are going there with the idea to win and be brave’ Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield on Sunday for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start. United are 18th in the Premier League and Liverpool fourth but the head coach will not accept any self-doubt. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and is keen to instil those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.
summary: Pochettino urges United to face Liverpool with no fear.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Rugby players await judge decision on concussion case
content:
Hundreds of former rugby players have filed legal action against the sport’s governing bodies, claiming they suffer neurological damage from professional negligence.  The defendants—World Rugby, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) and the Rugby Football League—argue that the cases should be struck out because of delays.  

The dispute was heard for two days at the Royal Courts of Justice.  The presiding judges, Senior Master Cook and Mr Justice Cotter, have now retired from the hearing to decide whether the plaintiffs’ claims can continue in their present form.  

The outcome will determine whether the players’ allegations of brain injury caused by negligence will proceed toward trial.
summary: Hundreds of former rugby players are suing World Rugby, the RFU, the WRU and the Rugby Football League for alleged brain injury caused by negligence. Senior Master Cook and Mr Justice Cotter have retired to decide whether the case can continue.
author: Guardian Sport

title: All Blacks aim for bounce‑back after shock defeat by Wales
content: New Zealand should provide a huge reaction to their shock defeat in Wales with enticing clash even more instructive From the Bay of Islands on the northern tip of New Zealand to Invercargill in the deep south, there is rare unanimity this week. Back in the day there would be parochial arguments about, say, the ratio of Aucklanders to Cantabrians in the starting XV. This time there is nationwide recognition that absolutely nothing matters beyond a bounce-back win for the boys in black on Saturday. It is the inevitable upshot of last weekend’s seismic defeat by Wales, a result that prompted Dave Rennie, the head coach, to admit his reshuffled team had “let ourselves and our country down”. The former All Black scrum-half Justin Marshall went a step further. “We were arrogant enough to think that we could make those changes and still protect our history, and now look what’s happened,” a wounded Marshall told the GBRNRZ podcast.
summary: The New Zealand All Blacks suffered a shock defeat to Wales, prompting head coach Dave Rennie to admit the team had let the country down. Former All Black scrum‑half Justin Marshall criticized the team's arrogance and said they had underestimated the impact of their changes.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Adam Hollioake eyed for Surrey head coach role as Finch takes MI London job
content:
Adam Hollioake is emerging as the favourite to become the new head coach of Surrey, a move that would mark a potential return for the former captain. The appointment comes as Aaron Finch is set to be appointed as coach of MI London, signaling a winter of change at the Oval.

Surrey is currently conducting a formal recruitment process that remains open. Internally, Hollioake is viewed as the leading candidate to replace Gareth Batty, who departed last month after four years to take up an assistant coach’s position with the Chennai Super Kings.
summary: Adam Hollioake is being considered to become Surrey's head coach. Aaron Finch will take the coaching position at MI London while Surrey continues an open recruitment process to replace former coach Gareth Batty, who departed for an assistant coach role at the Chennai Super Kings.
author: Guardian Sport

title: FIA to introduce permanent race stewards in 2027 season
content:
Formula One’s governing body, the FIA, has announced plans to recruit permanent staff, introducing full-time race stewards for the first time in the sport’s history starting with the 2027 season. This initiative aims to address ongoing controversy and follows long-standing debate within the sport regarding the consistency of race oversight.

Currently, each race relies on four volunteer stewards who change for every meeting. These individuals are selected from a pool of FIA choices, the local or regional sporting organization, and one former driver. Lewis Hamilton has previously criticized the inconsistency associated with this temporary stewarding model.
summary: FIA to introduce permanent race stewards in 2027 season.
author: Guardian Sport

title: OL Lyonnes defeat Arsenal to keep top spot in Women's Champions League
content:
Arsenal’s hopes of earning automatic progression to the Champions League quarter‑finals were dashed by OL Lyonnes, as the French side continued their statement form in Europe.  

The match at Meadow Park ended with goals from Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay, one in each half, giving Lyonnes a decisive victory. Lyonnes remain top of the league table and have not conceded a goal in the league phase, with one game still remaining.
summary: Arsenal lost to OL Lyonnes at Meadow Park, ending their hopes of automatic progression to the Champions League quarter-finals. Jule Brand and Melchie Dumornay scored for Lyonnes, who remain top of the table and have not conceded a goal in the league phase with one game remaining.
author: Guardian Sport

title: UEFA Suspends England's One-Match Away Ticket Ban, Fines FA £12,500 for Offensive Chants
content: Ban by Uefa is suspended for two years Uefa also fines FA £12,500 for offensive chants England have been handed a ­suspended ­one-match ban on away ticket sales by Uefa in relation to “­racist and/or ­discriminatory” behaviour by fans at Sunday’s 3-2 Nations League victory over Spain. The punishment is suspended for two years. Uefa has also fined the Football Association €15,000 (£12,500), with the behaviour in question believed to be the chant of “Fuck the pope and the IRA” at the ­Metropolitano ­Stadium in Madrid. A further charge in the next two years could trigger a ban on away fans for a competitive game.
summary: Ban by Uefa is suspended for two years Uefa also fines FA £12,500 for offensive chants England have been handed a ­suspended ­one-match ban on away ticket sales by Uefa in relation to “­racist and/or ­discriminatory” behaviour by fans at Sunday’s 3-2 Nations League victory over Spain. The punishment is suspended for two years.
author: Guardian Sport

title: World No. 1 Alexander Zverev aims to be pain‑free after beating Arthur Fils at ATP Finals
content: World number one Alexander Zverev says he will do "everything I can to be pain-free" after hurting his ankle during his ATP Finals victory over Arthur Fils.
summary: World number one Alexander Zverev said he will do everything he can to be pain‑free after hurting his ankle. He won his ATP Finals match against Arthur Fils.
author: BBC Sport

title: Shevchenko Accuses Mudryk's Camp of Baseless Slander Over Drug Test Claim
content: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko has accused Tottenham winger Mykhailo Mudryk of baseless slander. Mudryk, who is on‑loan to Tottenham, had blamed his failed drugs test on the national football association.
summary: Ukraine great Andriy Shevchenko accuses Mykhailo Mudryk of 'baseless slander'. The accusation followed Mudryk's claim that his failed drugs test was due to the nation's football association.
author: BBC Sport

title: Agnew questions Cummins' ability to lead Australia to Ashes amid sandpapergate
content: Jonathan Agnew has expressed uncertainty about Pat Cummins’ ability to lead Australia into next summer’s Ashes series in England, citing the latest developments in the sandpapergate scandal. Agnew’s comment highlights concerns over Cummins’ leadership amid the controversy.
summary: Jonathan Agnew says he struggles to see how Pat Cummins can lead Australia into next summer's Ashes series in England. This doubt follows the latest developments in the sandpapergate scandal.
author: BBC Sport

title: California Gov.-elect Becerra Calls for Charges Against Humans Behind AI Cyberattacks
content: California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra (D) said on Thursday that if the AI‑driven cyberattacks observed so far were carried out by humans, criminal charges would be filed against those individuals. He made the remark during an interview at Politico Pub at the National Governors Association event.
summary: California Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra said that if AI cyberattacks were carried out by humans, criminal charges would be filed. He made the remarks in an interview at Politico Pub at the National Governors Association’s event.
author: The Hill

title: Judge rules Trump’s defamation case against New York Times, Penguin Random House may proceed
content: President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The New York Times and publisher Penguin Random House can proceed, a federal judge ruled Thursday. The ruling is a victory for Trump in his effort to label the news outlet’s reporting about him as misinformation. Trump’s suit centers on a 2024 book written by Times reporters Russ Buettner and Susanne Craig.
summary: Judge rules Trump’s defamation case against New York Times, Penguin Random House may proceed.
author: The Hill

title: One company bids to mine off coast of American Samoa after Trump push
content: Wetstone US Ventures has provisionally secured two leases to mine off the coast of American Samoa, becoming the sole bidder in a process overseen by the Marine Minerals Administration. The bid comes amid the Trump administration’s push for offshore mining.
summary: One company has bid and provisionally won the rights to mine off the coast of American Samoa as the Trump administration pushes for offshore mining. Wetstone US Ventures provisionally acquired the two leases to mine off the coast, a spokesperson for the Marine Minerals Administration (MMA) said.
author: The Hill

title: Sen. Fetterman says he’s considering a 2028 reelection bid
content: Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) hinted at running for reelection in 2028, saying he is “considering things.” “I am considering things,” Fetterman said when MS NOW reporter Mychael Schnell asked if he is going to run in 2028. When the reporter asked if he is worried about a primary challenger in 2028, Fetterman responded saying, “Oh…
summary: Sen. Fetterman says he’s considering a 2028 reelection bid.
author: The Hill

title: Lawmakers urge Army to postpone Iowa lead bomb detonation over late communication
content: Federal and state lawmakers are urging the Army to postpone its planned detonation of a lead azide bomb in Iowa, citing late communication on the event. “The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be government’s top concern,” Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) wrote on social media. “An unacceptable lack of communication and…
summary: Federal and state lawmakers are urging the Army to postpone the planned detonation of a lead azide bomb in Iowa because of late communication. Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand (D) posted on social media that the safety of Iowans should be the government’s top concern and that there is an unacceptable lack of communication.
author: The Hill

title: Sen. Josh Hawley says he has thinking to do on possible 2028 presidential run
content: Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) left the door open to a 2028 presidential bid Thursday despite seemingly ruling one out before the midterms. Asked by The Associated Press about a possible run for president, Hawley said he has some “thinking to do.” “After this most recent election, I think everybody that cares about the future of…
summary: Sen. Josh Hawley, a Republican from Missouri, told the Associated Press on Thursday that he is keeping a 2028 presidential bid open. He said he has “thinking to do” after the most recent election.
author: The Hill

title: Van Hollen challenges Schumer for Senate Democratic leadership
content: Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D‑Md.) has announced a challenge to Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) for the top spot in the Senate Democratic Caucus. Van Hollen is backing a populist approach, outlining progressive economic positions to support his bid. The announcement was presented by Bitget.
summary: Presented by Bitget. {beacon} Business & Economy Business & Economy The Big Story Van Hollen backs populism in challenge to Schumer Sen.
author: The Hill

title: GOP Senators Oppose Funding Bills Containing Hemp Recriminalization Language
content: Two Republican senators have stated they will not support any government funding bill that includes language delaying or reversing the recriminalization of intoxicating hemp products. This position was highlighted in a report by the Coalition to Strengthen America’s Healthcare regarding the potential impact on federal funding.
summary: A pair of GOP senators say they won’t support any government funding bill if it includes language that delays or reverses the recriminalization of intoxicating hemp products. The stance was announced after bipartisan legislation was introduced.
author: The Hill

title: Rep. Gregory Meeks Questions Trump’s Achievements in Xi-Putin Summit
content: Rep. Gregory Meeks, a top House Democrat, has questioned the outcomes of President Trump’s summit with Chinese and Russian leaders. Meeks raised concerns regarding the impact of the meeting on U.S. alliances. Additionally, he addressed issues of Chinese espionage in connection with the Nvidia scandal.
summary: Rep. Gregory Meeks Questions Trump’s Achievements in Xi-Putin Summit.
author: NPR Politics

title: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark stresses Democratic unity
content: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark highlighted the Democratic Party’s ambitious agenda while acknowledging divisions within its ranks as the party prepares to take control of the House. The remarks were accompanied by an image credited to Anna Moneymaker.
summary: Incoming House majority leader Katherine Clark discusses the party's ambitious agenda. She also addresses divisions within the Democratic ranks.
author: NPR Politics

title: Anthropic raises more than $100B in IPO. And, Dems nominate Jeffries for House speaker
content: Anthropic completed a record-breaking initial public offering, raising more than $100 billion despite growing concerns about a potential AI bubble. Separately, Hakeem Jeffries has been nominated for the position of House Speaker, a role that could make him the first Black individual to hold that office.
summary: Despite growing concern over a possible AI bubble, Anthropic had a record-breaking initial public offering. And, Hakeem Jeffries could become the first Black Speaker of the House.
author: NPR Politics

title: Democrats win 56% of House votes, 14-point lead the widest in 50 years
content: The recent midterm elections saw Democrats receive 56 % of the vote in House races, while Republicans garnered 42 %. This 14‑point margin represents the widest victory for either party in 50 years, a record not seen since the post‑Watergate era.
summary: Democrats received 56% of the votes in House races, while Republicans received 42%. The 14-point margin is the widest win for either party in 50 years since after Watergate.
author: NPR Politics

title: Scott Colom becomes Mississippi's first Black U.S. Senator in 150 years
content:
Scott Colom has become the first Black U.S. Senator from Mississippi in nearly 150 years, a milestone that has drawn national attention.  

Scholars and Mississippi natives Eddie Glaude and Kiese Laymon have reflected on the historic significance of Colom’s victory, framing it as a moment larger than Barack Obama’s election.
summary: Scott Colom is now this Southern state's first Black U. S.
author: NPR Politics

title: Federal judges delay Trump's arch and pause golf course redesign
content:
A federal judge has delayed construction of Trump’s arch twice.  

Another judge is keeping East Potomac Park open, while a federal arts panel gave mixed feedback on the proposed golf‑course redesign Thursday.
summary: A federal judge has delayed construction of Trump's arch twice, and another judge is keeping East Potomac Park open. A federal arts panel gave mixed feedback on the proposed golf course redesign on Thursday.
author: NPR Politics

title: Brexit debate returns as UK‑EU discussion resurfaces
content: The debate over whether the United Kingdom should remain in the European Union has returned to the public agenda. According to the report, many of the personalities and arguments that shaped the original Brexit discussion are re‑emerging, and observers note growing nerves about what may follow.
summary: The debate over the UK’s membership in the EU is back on the agenda. Many of the names and arguments that defined the original Brexit period are reappearing, prompting nerves about what happens next.
author: BBC Politics

title: Cop31 draft removes fossil fuel references, threatens 'ghost' summit
content: Draft agreement also fails to show how developing countries will receive financial help to deal with climate crisis Cop31 live – latest updates Every mention of fossil fuels has been expunged from the draft outcome of global climate talks, which were approaching their final hours on Thursday night, threatening to turn the UN summit into what campaigners called a “ghost Cop”. The second draft of the key text, released on Thursday afternoon and setting out the main commitments from the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, removed a pledge to phase out fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification, while other parallel texts failed to flesh out how developing countries would receive the financial help they needed to deal with the climate crisis.
summary: The draft outcome of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey has removed all references to fossil fuels and weakened electrification goals. Parallel texts do not explain how developing countries will receive the financial help needed to address the climate crisis.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Native communities in US southwest seek recovery after El Niño‑intensified flooding
content:
Severe flooding in Shiprock, New Mexico, has left the town submerged in toxic water, prompting residents and local groups to unite in recovery efforts. The disaster followed unprecedented rainfall across the Four Corners region of the south‑west United States, which authorities said heightened the risk of flooding along the San Juan River.

On the night of 23 October, 67‑year‑old Jimmie Goodman was awakened by his sister, who was still recuperating from back surgery and struggling to sleep. Goodman recalled that local officials had warned of a potential surge from the San Juan River. He stepped outside to see the water surge directly toward their home. The river makes a sharp 90‑degree turn near the couple’s house, located in a Navajo Housing Authority residential neighborhood, and the surge missed the house by about 50 feet.

The community is now working to address the damage and the hazardous conditions left by the flood.
summary: Severe flooding on 23 October submerged Shiprock, New Mexico, with toxic water from the San Juan River after unprecedented rain across the Four Corners region. Residents, including 67‑year‑old Jimmie Goodman, banded together after authorities warned of the river’s risk, with the surge missing their house by about 50 feet.
author: Guardian Environment

title: US Army to Detonate 5 Tons of Bomb‑Making Chemicals in Iowa, Residents Warned of Lead Dust
content:
Officials have announced that the U.S. Army plans to detonate approximately five tons of bomb‑making chemicals at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The chemicals have become unusable and could explode if moved, prompting worries among residents in south‑eastern Iowa about a potential cloud of lead dust that could cause environmental contamination and health problems.

The detonation is scheduled for Friday. Residents in the nearby town of Middletown are advised to begin vacating the area that morning. If they are unable to leave, officials recommend staying inside and keeping windows and doors closed to reduce exposure to the expected toxic plume. Some schools in the area will also be closed as part of the precautionary measures.
summary: US Army to Detonate 5 Tons of Bomb‑Making Chemicals in Iowa, Residents Warned of Lead Dust.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Research Finds Baby's Transition to Solid Foods Shapes Lifelong Taste Preferences
content: New research in mice indicates that a baby’s transition from breast milk or formula to solid foods is the likely “sweet spot” for introducing nutritional variety. This period may influence lifelong taste preferences by rewiring brain circuits.
summary: New research in mice suggests that a baby's transition from breast milk or formula to solid foods is the likely sweet spot for introducing nutritional variety. This transition may influence lifelong taste preferences by rewiring brain circuits.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Common type 1 diabetes score misses over half of partial remissions in youth with overweight or obesity
content: A Baylor College of Medicine–led team is raising awareness about the application of insulin dose-adjusted hemoglobin A1c (IDAA1c) values when screening for partial type 1 diabetes remission in youth with overweight or obesity. The study was published in Diabetes Care.
summary: A Baylor College of Medicine–led team is raising awareness about using IDAA1c values to screen for partial type 1 diabetes remission in overweight or obese youth. The study was published in Diabetes Care.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Lyme disease infection causes lasting bone marrow changes, study finds
content: A new study led by researchers at Tufts University School of Medicine reports that infection with Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium that causes Lyme disease, can leave lasting changes in the immune system even after the infection is treated. The researchers found that these changes occur in the bone marrow, the site where many of the body’s immune cells are produced. The study suggests that the altered bone‑marrow environment may affect how the immune system responds to future threats.
summary: Researchers at Tufts University School of Medicine found that infection with Borrelia burgdorferi can leave lasting changes in the immune system after treatment. The changes occur in the bone marrow, where many immune cells are made, potentially altering future immune responses.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study says cancer cases in England's trans community may more than double in 10 years
content: A study led by Queen Mary University of London warns that new cancer cases each year among transgender and gender‑diverse people in England could more than double over the next decade.
summary: A study led by Queen Mary University of London examined cancer incidence among transgender and gender-diverse people in England. It found that the number of new cancer cases each year could more than double over the next decade.
author: Medical Xpress

title: University of Tokyo researchers identify brain region that processes both math and language
content:
Researchers from the University of Tokyo and other institutions have addressed a long‑standing debate in neuroscience regarding how the brain processes math and language. Two opposing views have suggested that each function is confined to distinct brain regions or that the functions are integrated in a single area.  

A new study, published in Science Advances, demonstrates that both perspectives are partially correct. The research confirms the existence of specialized areas for math and for language while also identifying a previously unrecognized region that processes both mathematical and linguistic information.
summary: Researchers from the University of Tokyo published new findings in Science Advances that show both specialized and shared brain regions for math and language. The study identifies a newly discovered region that processes both math and language.
author: Medical Xpress

title: R21 malaria vaccine reduces infection odds by up to 70% in community mass vaccination
content: A new study published in The Lancet reports that vaccinating whole communities with the malaria vaccine R21 before the rainy season, in addition to existing malaria control tools, can reduce the odds of infection by up to 70%. The findings highlight the potential of seasonal mass vaccination to significantly lower malaria incidence.
summary: A new study published in The Lancet found that vaccinating whole communities with the malaria vaccine R21 before the rainy season can reduce the odds of infection by up to 70%. The vaccination was carried out alongside existing malaria control tools.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study: Seeing social media as having one purpose makes it feel like a better place to reconnect
content: A recent study suggests that viewing social media as having a single purpose can make it feel like a better place to reconnect. The research notes that platforms that perform many functions at once may feel awkward when users try to reach out to an old friend.
summary: You can't be all things to all people, and the same apparently holds true for social media platforms. At its core, social media is supposed to be, well, social.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Swiss tennis player Leandro Riedi credits sport as savior after suicide attempt
content:
Swiss tennis player Leandro Riedi said that tennis was his “saviour” after he attempted to take his own life.  
The attempt occurred shortly before Wimbledon qualifying began in June 2024, prompting Riedi to credit the sport with helping him recover.
summary: Swiss tennis player Leandro Riedi attempted to take his own life shortly before Wimbledon qualifying began in June 2024. He says the sport was his savior.
author: BBC Health

title: Covid inquiry urges UK–Ireland pandemic coordination in future
content:
The Covid inquiry has called for future pandemic coordination between the UK and Ireland.  

In its latest report on test and trace, the inquiry noted that cooperation is required to make border control measures effective and operable in practice.
summary: The Covid inquiry's latest report on the test and trace programme calls for cooperation to ensure border control measures are effective and operable in practice. It urges UK–Ireland pandemic coordination in the future.
author: BBC Health

title: Bank of England faces £160m headquarters revamp cost and delay concerns
content: UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home. A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.
summary: Bank of England faces £160m headquarters revamp cost and delay concerns.
author: Guardian Business

title: US Judge Allows Trump's $15bn Defamation Lawsuit Against New York Times to Proceed
content:
A federal judge in Florida has allowed Donald Trump’s $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House to proceed. US District Judge Steven Merryday in Tampa ruled on Thursday that the core defamation claims may move forward, marking a victory for the US president in his legal campaign against media companies he accuses of unfair treatment. Trump alleges defamation by three Times reporters and the book publisher.

The judge dismissed two specific claims within the suit while permitting the central allegations to advance. This decision represents a significant step in the ongoing legal dispute between the president and the news outlets.
summary: Donald Trump’s $15bn defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House may proceed after a federal judge in Florida ruled it can move forward. Judge Steven Merryday dismissed two claims in the suit but allowed the core defamation claims to continue.
author: Guardian Business

title: Union leaders from 19 countries urge governments to review Amazon public contracts
content: Union leaders from 19 countries urge reassessment of ties to Amazon, citing company’s poor record on worker rights More than 30 labor union leaders from 19 countries are calling on governments to review their public contracts with Amazon and Amazon Web Services, citing the company’s poor record on worker rights and collective bargaining, in an open letter published on Thursday. “Amazon’s consistent record of disrespect for workers’ fundamental rights should disqualify it from being awarded public contracts – its behaviour is fundamentally inconsistent with the shared democratic values of our countries,” the union leaders wrote.
summary: Union leaders from 19 countries urge governments to review Amazon public contracts.
author: Guardian Business

title: How microbes make drug-like chemicals without damaging themselves
content:
University of Michigan researchers discovered a mechanism that enables microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi to produce drug‑like molecules that can fight infections or kill cancer cells without damaging themselves.  

This finding shows how microbes synthesize potent compounds while protecting their own cellular integrity.
summary: University of Michigan researchers have discovered a mechanism that enables microscopic organisms like bacteria and fungi to produce drug-like molecules—compounds that can fight infections or kill cancer cells—without damaging themselves.
author: Phys.org

title: Some meerkats gain solo navigation skills that guide group movements
content: After emerging from their burrow each morning to warm in the early sun, meerkats focus on a single goal: finding food. The group heads out together, moving slowly along a shared route before returning home quickly at the end of the day. While the tight‑knit band navigates as one, some individuals gain extra experience by roaming solo, and that experience can influence the community’s overall maneuvers.
summary: After emerging from their burrow, meerkats collectively search for food. Individuals who roam alone develop navigation skills that influence the group's daily routes.
author: Phys.org

title: Osaka and UBC team develops polymer dots for imaging and light-triggered cancer killing
content:
A research team led by Professor Youhei Takeda of the University of Osaka, in collaboration with Professor Zachary M. Hudson of the University of British Columbia (UBC) in Canada, has created a new polymer material. The material emits fluorescence, enabling it to be used for cell imaging, and it can also kill cancer cells when activated by light.

The dual‑function polymer offers a simpler route to “nanotheranostic” technologies, which combine disease imaging and treatment in a single platform.
summary: Osaka and UBC team develops polymer dots for imaging and light-triggered cancer killing.
author: Phys.org

title: Cattails grow tiny “snorkels” to manipulate soil chemistry in marshes
content: Cattails are a common feature of both brackish and freshwater marshes, where they grow abundantly. In water‑logged soils, the plants confront low oxygen availability, a condition that threatens root respiration. To cope, cattails develop tiny “snorkel” structures that alter the surrounding soil chemistry, helping their roots obtain the oxygen they need.
summary: Cattails develop tiny snorkel-like structures that alter soil chemistry in wetlands. They thrive in both brackish and freshwater marshes despite roots needing oxygen in waterlogged soil.
author: Phys.org

title: Euclid's hunt for strong gravitational lenses begins successfully
content: Euclid’s search for strong gravitational lenses has begun strongly, according to the title. The accompanying text notes that if dark matter and dark energy were part of everyday life, we would be in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness, since 95 % of matter and energy would be invisible and undetectable, making it impossible to make sense of our surroundings.
summary: Euclid's hunt for strong gravitational lenses is off to a strong start. Dark matter and dark energy together comprise about 95% of the universe's matter and energy and are invisible.
author: Phys.org

title: Quantum statistics may explain strange metals, not collisions
content: In “strange metals” such as the copper‑oxide superconductors, electrical resistance increases linearly with temperature across a broad range, and electrons appear to shed momentum at the fastest rate allowed by quantum mechanics, known as the Planckian limit. Unlike ordinary metals, where electrons act as well‑defined particles that scatter off crystal imperfections or vibrations, these materials defy that picture. A new perspective suggests that the underlying cause may be rooted in quantum‑statistical effects rather than conventional electron collisions, although the precise mechanism remains an open question.
summary: Strange metals show a linear increase of electrical resistance with temperature across a broad range, and their electrons lose momentum at the Planckian limit. Researchers suggest the phenomenon may stem from quantum statistics rather than particle collisions.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists develop hollow “PAC‑MAN” capsules that filter particles in turbulent water
content: Scientists have engineered hollow capsules that feature a single opening and use turbulence in surrounding water to selectively filter particles. The capsules can ingest particles in a manner likened to PAC‑MAN eating dots, a capability that researchers suggest could be useful for filtration and drug‑delivery applications.
summary: Scientists have created hollow capsules with a single opening that can selectively filter particles using turbulence in water. The capsules can ingest particles like Pac‑Man and are seen as promising for filtration and drug delivery.
author: Phys.org

title: Tammy Nicholas's porcelain crab photo wins The Nature Conservancy Oceania Photo Contest
content:
The Nature Conservancy’s Oceania Photo Contest announced its overall winner as Tammy Nicholas. Her photograph, titled Porcelain Crab Feathered Feast, shows a porcelain crab catching plankton while half‑hidden in an anemone. The blue shadows in the image give it an otherworldly feel. Nicholas took the shot on a coral reef off Gili Air Island in Indonesia.

In the wildlife category, Crispin Middleton earned second prize with Ocean Drifter, a picture of a drifter or pelagic crab clinging to a piece of kelp near the Poor Knights Islands of New Zealand. The plants and fungi category was won by Vanessa Torres Macho’s Pendants, depicting water lilies growing in the Cenote Carwash near Tulum, Mexico. The water category’s second place went to Justin Tan’s Frenzy, showing sardines pursued by diving Cape gannets off Port St Johns in South Africa during the sardine run.

The people and nature category’s first prize was awarded to Vanessa Mignon’s Socialisation, an image of a researcher filming juvenile sperm whales and a calf off the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. Mignon noted that the filming was done under permit, though it is often conducted illegally. The contest is open only to residents of Australia, New Zealand, Papua New Guinea and the Solomon Islands, but photographs may be taken anywhere.
summary: Tammy Nicholas's porcelain crab photo wins The Nature Conservancy Oceania Photo Contest.
author: New Scientist

title: Researchers find woman who entered hibernation-like state for more than 30 years
content: Researchers studying donated brains discovered a woman who, for more than 30 years, entered a hibernation‑like state during winter.  During these prolonged periods of reduced activity, her body temperature fell as low as 31 °C.
summary: Researchers studying donated brains discovered a woman who entered prolonged, hibernation-like periods of reduced activity each winter for more than 30 years. In those episodes her body temperature dropped to as low as 31°C.
author: New Scientist

title: 8-metre extinct orca species from 2‑million‑year‑old North Sea suggests early marine‑mammal diet
content: A nearly 8‑metre‑long extinct orca species was discovered in the North Sea more than two million years ago. The find suggests that orcas adopted a marine‑mammal diet earlier than scientists had previously believed.
summary: A nearly 8‑metre‑long species of orca lived in the North Sea over 2 million years ago. Its discovery suggests orcas evolved a diet of marine mammals earlier than scientists thought.
author: New Scientist

title: California sues OpenAI over Hugging Face attack alleging unfair competition
content: California has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI for the Hugging Face incident Chris Jung/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Can you send a computer to jail? No, obviously not. That’s a stupid question. And yet it is one that AI firms seem to want us to ask when faced with tales of “rogue agents” breaking into other peoples’ computers. As is so often the case with our current AI moment, storytelling has got in the way of reality. Thankfully, that may be starting to change. This week, California announced that it is filing a lawsuit against OpenAI over an incident that occurred earlier this year, when another AI firm, Hugging Face, was hit by an attack that turned out to originate from OpenAI’s servers. The real reasons we keep seeing big tech outages – it isn’t just hackers In OpenAI’s telling, the Hugging Face hack was “driven by a combination of OpenAI models”, models that were “hyperfocused” on achieving a goal and found ways to “cheat” by stealing the answers for a test from Hugging Face’s servers. It is easy to come away with the impression that seemingly no humans were involved, and certainly not to blame. But in the words of California Attorney General Rob Bonta, the attack “was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability”, and he explicitly dismisses “science fiction fantasies of rogue AI systems run amok”. Advertisement Ever since the Hugging Face attack occurred, I have struggled to understand why OpenAI has yet to face legal consequences for what would seem to be a crime – unauthorised computer access under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act – if conducted by a human. So far, the legal answer to this seems to be a lack of intent, which the law requires, and it remains an untested legal question whether an AI can have intent, according to an analysis by US firm Ballard Spahr. California is instead bringing a civil suit, alleging that OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, which prohibits harmful or fraudulent business practices even when there is no intent to deceive. OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit. “This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab,” said OpenAI spokesperson Drew Pusateri. As legal defences go, “everyone is doing it” doesn’t seem like a very good one to me, but that will be for the courts to decide. What is clear is that we need an agreed understanding of liability when it comes to AI, but what I don’t think we need are special AI laws when our existing ones work just fine. For example, in 2024, Air Canada was held liable for misleading information given to a customer by its AI chatbot. A tribunal ruled that Air Canada had effectively tried to argue that the chatbot was a legally separate entity that it was not responsible for – an argument that did not wash. In my view, any similar claims that AI can have its own legal agency should be dismissed. The argument that an AI is a legal actor serves AI companies in two ways, neither of which benefits society at large. The first is that it attempts to swerve responsibility, while the second is that it adds to the story of AI being an all-powerful, unknowable being. That second story is at the heart of the current AI revolution, but it isn’t one we have to listen to. How preppers plan to save us if the whole internet collapses I prefer a different argument. For the past year or so, Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor at Princeton University have put forward the idea of “ AI as Normal Technology ” – transformative, yes, in the same way as the internet or electricity, but not something that requires re-engineering the ordinary functions of society. As a normal technology, normal laws can apply. Writing about the Hugging Face attack earlier this year, the pair said that “AI companies should be liable for what their agents do” and, like Bonta, blame OpenAI’s internal culture and lack of human oversight for the incident. The most high-profile example of existing laws being applied to AI companies is a class-action lawsuit against Anthropic, alleging that the firm used pirated copies of books to train its Claude AI models. Anthropic settled, and is now in the process of paying out to affected authors from a $1.5 billion fund. The wider question of whether training an AI on copyrighted material is illegal or counts as fair use remains open, and I really can’t believe that, four years after the launch of ChatGPT, we don’t yet have an answer to what is probably one of the most fundamental legal disputes of our time. OpenAI has previously said it would be “ impossible ” to create the kind of AI we have now without using copyrighted material, so this is an existential question for the AI firms. Existing laws can also be tweaked to make it clear that they apply to AI. The European Union has done just that, updating a 1985 consumer rights directive to produce the 2024 Product Liability Directive, which explicitly makes it clear that software, including artificial intelligence, is a product and that people writing software are liable for any defects. The law doesn’t come into force until 9 December, when EU members must implement it, and it remains to be seen how it might be used against AI companies. In other words, we don’t have to try to send a computer to jail. We’ve got humans who should be liable instead. As Bonta says, “While the technology OpenAI develops may be new, California’s prohibitions against conduct that harms the public and laws against unfair, deceptive, and fraudulent business practices are not.” Further AI reading After much fanfare, Anthropic has listed on the stock market at $83 a share, giving it a valuation of around $1.5 trillion. It is the second big AI firm to go public this year, following SpaceXAI in June. The Economist has a great piece on whether the AI industry can ever make enough money to survive. It calculates that it must produce $3 trillion in revenue by 2030 to cover the costs of planned data centres. That is roughly equivalent to a tenth of all wages in high-income countries, or similar to the amount spent on food. Are people really going to buy as much AI as they do food? The Cambridge Dictionary has named “ human ” as word of the year, as a pushback against the growth of AI. It feels a bit like trying too hard to be relevant, in my view. As the COP31 climate summit continues, only nine countries have signed a pledge aimed at limiting the environmental impact of AI. As I have written previously, we cannot afford to run this 21st-century technology on a 20th-century energy supply.
summary: California has filed a lawsuit against OpenAI concerning an incident in which Hugging Face was attacked by activity originating from OpenAI’s servers. The suit alleges OpenAI created a risk to public safety and violated the state’s Unfair Competition Law, and OpenAI has objected to the lawsuit.
author: New Scientist

title: Study finds U.S. data centers cause 650 premature deaths via distant air pollution
content:
A new study by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology quantifies how the rapid expansion of artificial‑intelligence data centers harms air quality and public health far beyond the sites of the facilities themselves. By linking hourly electricity demand from data centers to emissions from generators across the United States, the team estimates that the additional power use in 2023 produced roughly 650 premature deaths nationwide—about 5.3 percent of all electricity‑related mortality in the country.

The researchers built a modeling framework that tracks how data‑center electricity demand propagates through the nation’s interconnected grid and how resulting emissions travel under varying atmospheric conditions. The model incorporates emissions of nitrogen oxides (NOx) and sulfur dioxide (SO₂) from more than 10,000 generators, then feeds these data into a chemical‑transport model that simulates formation of fine particulate matter (PM₂.5) and ground‑level ozone (smog). Translating the added pollution into health outcomes using epidemiological evidence yields an estimate of 513 premature deaths from PM₂.5 and 137 from smog.

Although the bulk of data‑center electricity consumption was concentrated in northern Virginia and Texas, the highest per‑capita mortality rates appeared in Midwestern states such as Iowa, Nevada, South Dakota and Kansas. The mismatch arises because generators that respond to demand spikes in Virginia often lie in the Ohio Valley, where older coal‑ and natural‑gas plants emit more pollutants. Atmospheric transport further carries these emissions into downwind regions, where conditions—such as agricultural ammonia—enhance PM₂.5 formation.

The study’s senior author, Professor Noelle Selin of MIT’s Institute for Data, Systems, and Society and the Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, emphasizes that health impacts extend beyond communities neighboring data centers. Rural populations, in particular, face higher mortality risk because of the spatial distribution of power plants and prevailing weather patterns. The authors suggest that siting and operational decisions for data centers should incorporate air‑quality considerations alongside traditional factors like land and energy costs.

Future work will explore the air‑quality effects of onsite power generation at data centers and assess how flexible operation schedules might mitigate emissions. The research, co‑authored with MIT graduate student Yuang (Albert) Chen and collaborators at the University of California, Irvine, and Yale University, appears in the journal Environmental Research Letters and was funded in part by the MIT Energy Initiative Society of Energy Scholars and the MIT Martin Family Society of Fellows for Sustainability.
summary: MIT researchers estimate that extra air pollution from data‑center electricity use in 2023 led to about 650 premature deaths in the United States. The highest per‑capita mortality rates occurred in Midwestern states despite most data‑center power demand being in Virginia and Texas, showing how grid emissions and atmospheric conditions spread health impacts.
author: MIT News

title: MIT engineers create dry, stretchy material to replace ultrasound gel
content:
Engineers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and the Singapore‑MIT Alliance for Research and Technology’s Wearable Imaging for Transforming Elderly Care (SMART WITEC) project have created a dry, stretchy polymer that can replace the conventional ultrasound coupling gel. The new material is designed to transmit ultrasound waves efficiently while remaining stable without the need for liquid replenishment, a limitation that has hindered long‑term wearable ultrasound devices.

Current practice requires a cold, water‑based gel to fill microscopic gaps between a probe and a patient’s skin, ensuring clear images. The MIT team’s earlier wearable patches used a hydrogel layer, but the gel dried out within a day or two, reducing acoustic performance. By engineering a solid polymer with a “bottlebrush” molecular architecture—backbone chains bearing dense side‑chain bristles—the researchers reduced friction between polymer chains, allowing the material to behave acoustically like a gel while staying dry from the start.

Laboratory tests on synthetic “phantom” models showed that the material transmitted ultrasound waves clearly for about nine days of continuous operation. In a treadmill experiment, a volunteer wearing a patch of the new polymer on the chest experienced no sweat buildup, whereas a conventional silicone rubber patch became water‑logged. A field demonstration involved affixing a key‑fob‑sized patch with an integrated probe to a volunteer’s neck; the device recorded uninterrupted blood‑flow images during a 30‑minute bike ride across the Cambridge‑Charlestown area.

The study, reported in Science, lists postdoctoral researchers Shu Wang and Runze Li as co‑lead authors, with additional contributions from MIT faculty Xuanhe Zhao, Chen Gong, Won Jun Song, and collaborators Zihan Tang and Ying Li (University of Wisconsin‑Madison), Chwee Teck Lim (National University of Singapore), and Xiaodong Chen (Nanyang Technological University). Zhao, Chen and Lim serve as co‑lead principal investigators of the SMART WITEC group. The work was supported in part by the Singapore‑MIT Alliance for Research and Technology and the MIT Health and Life Sciences Collaborative.
summary: MIT and Singapore-MIT Alliance researchers developed a dry, rubbery material that can replace the wet gel used in ultrasound imaging. The material enabled a wearable ultrasound patch to produce clear images continuously for nine days, even during vigorous exercise.
author: MIT News

title: MIT and Dana‑Farber researchers find code sharing rare in clinical prediction studies
content: The data and code that underpin a research study can tell us what was actually done, and how. In a medical study, for example, how were patients selected for inclusion? How were missing values handled? How were the results evaluated? Access to a study's data and code help researchers to answer these questions, to examine the methods, and to build on the work. “Studies involve many choices about how to prepare data, develop models, and evaluate performance. These are sometimes called ‘researcher degrees of freedom,’” says Tom Pollard, a research scientist at MIT's Laboratory for Computational Physiology and Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory. “The choices we make affect the results, and a methods section in a paper can only capture so much detail.” While sharing code can be a first step, in order for code to be understood and reused, it must be sufficiently structured and described. The problem is that, right now, there is little guidance for researchers on what constitutes a well-organized, well-described collection of code. This is where an international team led by researchers at MIT and Dana-Farber Cancer Institute sought to help, by examining how code is currently shared in clinical prediction studies. Such studies develop or evaluate models to estimate patient outcomes, such as the risk of developing a disease. Because these models inform decisions about patient care, researchers need to be able to scrutinize how they were built and tested. Using large language models (LLMs), the researchers examined nearly 4,000 papers to identify statements about shared code. They then followed the statements to assess hundreds of associated code repositories. Their review revealed two key gaps: Code sharing remains uncommon, and making code public does not consistently mean providing the documentation and supporting information needed for reuse. The open-access findings, recently published in Nature Medicine, are informing TRIPOD-Code, a reporting guideline being developed to clarify what researchers should share. Following the code TRIPOD-Code builds on TRIPOD and TRIPOD+AI, checklists that help researchers report how clinical prediction models were developed and evaluated. To understand current code-sharing practices, the team identified studies citing either guideline. The review included almost 4,000 studies that developed, updated, or validated prediction models, and whose full texts were available through PubMed Central’s open-access collection. “The challenge was that the information was highly inconsistent. First, we had to identify whether or not a paper shared code” says Thomas Sounack, the study’s first author. He adds that authors “discuss and link to code from a paper in many different ways.” The team used an LLM to help screen papers, identify statements about code availability, and extract links. Software then retrieved the linked repositories — online collections of code and related files — for further assessment. The workflow went beyond checking whether a link existed. It also assessed repositories against characteristics such as completeness of documentation, software requirements, and terms of reuse. “The real benefit of LLMs is their ability to process unstructured information such as text. These models helped us work with information that was scattered across papers and software repositories, rather than neatly organized in a table,” says Pollard, who is a senior author of the study. “That allowed us to examine how code was being shared in much more detail across a large collection of studies.” Human reviewers evaluated the work of the LLMs. Two researchers independently checked 500 papers and a separate sample of repositories, resolving disagreements before comparing their assessments with the automated results. Agreement was stronger for concrete characteristics, such as whether a license file was present, than for judgments about the adequacy of documentation. Because classification errors remain possible, the authors emphasize the overall patterns rather than treating every count as exact. Inconsistent code sharing Only about 1 in 8 studies reported sharing code. Where code was shared, the contents of repositories varied widely. Some repositories were “extremely well-organized and -documented, while others gave almost no guidance at all,” Sounack says. Good code sharing, he explains, means “giving enough information to understand what the code does and be able to run it to reproduce the results reported in the paper.” Practices also varied substantially across journals and countries. Among journals, the proportion of studies sharing code ranged from zero to more than 70 percent. Some journals with low sharing rates nevertheless had written code-sharing policies, suggesting that policies alone may not be enough to motivate code sharing. The review also helped to identify examples of effective practice. Some researchers, for example, provided synthetic datasets to assist with code reuse where the original patient records could not be shared publicly. Setting a standard for code sharing Researchers who share code are already making an effort to make their work transparent. But clinical prediction research brings together people from medicine, statistics, and computer science, whose expectations for documenting and sharing code may differ. TRIPOD-Code aims to establish a consensus. Through an expert review process, the team is developing guidance on which elements of shared analytical code should be considered essential. “We want to give researchers practical guidance on how to share code, and give journals clearer expectations to communicate to authors,” Pollard says. “The review gives us evidence to inform those discussions."
summary: Researchers at MIT and Dana‑Farber used large language models to review nearly 4,000 clinical prediction studies, finding that only about one in eight shared code and that many repositories lacked sufficient documentation. Their findings are informing the development of TRIPOD‑Code, a reporting guideline to clarify what code should be shared.
author: MIT News

title: Field Museum scientists identify new 300‑million‑year‑old amphibian ancestor
content: Scientists at Chicago’s Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor that lived more than 300 million years ago in a swampy landscape that covered the region. The find offers new clues about the early evolution of frogs and salamanders.
summary: Scientists at the Field Museum have identified a previously unrecognized species of ancient amphibian ancestor that lived more than 300 million years ago. The discovery offers new clues about frog and salamander evolution and indicates the Chicago area was a steamy, swampy landscape at that time.
author: Science Daily

title: Sodium particles cause hydrogen flames to shift from orange to nearly invisible
content: Hydrogen flames can change from a bright orange hue to being almost invisible when trace amounts of sodium are present in the surrounding air. Scientists note that this finding may improve safety in future hydrogen‑powered stoves and ovens by allowing visual flame detection to be replaced with dedicated sensors.
summary: Hydrogen flames can shift from bright orange to nearly invisible due to tiny amounts of sodium floating in the air. Scientists say the discovery could make future hydrogen-powered stoves and ovens safer by replacing visual flame detection with specialized sensors.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find tiny bacterium under skin of deep‑sea sea pigs
content: Scientists have identified a previously unknown bacterium living beneath the skin of deep‑sea organisms called sea pigs, indicating an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe possesses an unusually small genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA encodes surface proteins, some of which are exceptionally large. Researchers suggest the bacterium relies heavily on its sea‑pig host for survival, while the benefit to the host remains unclear. The discovery highlights a novel host‑microbe relationship in the deep‑sea environment.
summary: Researchers discovered a bacterium living beneath the skin of deep‑sea creatures known as sea pigs. The microbe has an unusually small genome with over a quarter of its DNA dedicated to large surface proteins and appears to depend heavily on its host, while its benefit to the sea pig remains unknown.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists study why Ozempic and Wegovy cause varied weight‑loss results
content: Ozempic and Wegovy have been shown to produce dramatic weight loss for some individuals while yielding disappointing results for others. Scientists are investigating whether a hidden energy‑saving response in the body might explain these differing outcomes and could help develop more effective, personalized weight‑loss treatments.
summary: Ozempic and Wegovy produce dramatic weight loss for some people but disappointing results for others. Scientists are investigating whether a hidden energy‑saving response in the body could explain the difference and enable more effective, personalized weight‑loss treatments.
author: Science Daily

title: Gut bacteria produce sulfur gases that cause terrible‑smelling farts
content: The unpleasant odor of flatulence comes from tiny amounts of sulfur‑containing gases that gut bacteria generate while digesting food. Scientists explain that certain foods boost these gases, that a loud fart is not always the smelliest, and that human noses have evolved to detect such potent odors.
summary: The secret behind truly terrible‑smelling farts is tiny amounts of sulfur‑containing gases produced by gut bacteria as they digest food. Scientists explain why certain foods increase the odor, why loud farts are not always the stinkiest, and how human noses evolved to detect these strong smells.
author: Science Daily

title: Brain study finds similar neural activity for free and forced decisions
content: New research shows that the brain uses surprisingly similar neural processes for both free choices and forced decisions, with activity building toward a decision before action occurs. The finding challenges assumptions about free will while indicating that personal preferences and experiences continue to shape what people choose.
summary: New research shows the brain uses surprisingly similar neural processes for free choices and forced decisions, with activity building toward a decision before we act. The finding challenges assumptions about free will and suggests personal preferences and experiences still shape what we choose.
author: Science Daily

title: Extinct Peruvian pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo had extremely crooked face
content: A 6‑million‑year‑old whale discovered in Peru has been identified as the extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo. Researchers noted that its skull is dramatically distorted, with an enormous downward‑curving snout, giving it a face that appears extremely crooked. The unusual asymmetry led scientists initially to suspect post‑mortem damage, but further analysis suggests the shape was a genuine evolutionary adaptation for hunting along the seafloor. The team proposes that this whale may represent the most asymmetrical facial structure recorded in any mammal.
summary: The extinct pygmy sperm whale Scaphokogia huachafo, which lived about 6 million years ago, was discovered in Peru. Its skull shows an enormous downward‑curving snout and extreme facial asymmetry that researchers interpret as an adaptation for hunting along the seafloor.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find fungal toxins in all 212 UK plant‑based foods tested
content: A new study examined 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the United Kingdom, covering categories such as meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk and soy milk. Researchers found that each product contained at least one potentially harmful fungal toxin, known as a mycotoxin. The study notes that mycotoxins are natural compounds that can contaminate grains, legumes and seeds during farming and storage.
summary: Researchers tested 212 vegan and vegetarian products sold in the UK, including meat alternatives, oat milk, almond milk and soy milk, and found each contained at least one fungal toxin. The toxins, known as mycotoxins, are naturally occurring compounds that can contaminate grains, legumes and seeds during farming and storage.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists grow potatoes in simulated lunar soil, see them as key moon food source
content:
A new scientific report claims that potatoes could become a crucial food source for future lunar missions. The study documents that the tuber was successfully cultivated in simulated lunar soil, demonstrating that it can grow under conditions similar to those on the Moon.

According to the report, sustaining human life during prolonged lunar exploration will rely on life‑support systems that can produce food locally. Potatoes, with their high yield and nutritional value, are identified as an ideal candidate for such systems.

The research was conducted by scientists on a project backed by NASA, which concluded that the successful growth of potatoes in lunar‑soil simulant supports the feasibility of in‑situ food production for a future Moon base.
summary: Scientists reported that potatoes were successfully cultivated in simulated lunar soil. The Nasa‑backed project concluded the humble potato could be a key food source for a future moon base.
author: Guardian Science

title: Voyager 1 reaches one light‑day distance from Earth
content: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech NASA’s Voyager 1 probe, humanity’s farthest-flying spacecraft, has reached one light-day from Earth, after more than 49 years of constant travel. A light-day is the distance light travels in 24 hours, equaling about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). The spacecraft achieved the milestone at 2:16 a. M. PST (5:16 a. M. EST) Nov. 18. Voyager team members at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California, managed by Caltech, heard from the probe 24 hours later, the time it took for the spacecraft’s radio signal traveling at the speed of light to reach Earth, early Thursday. “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.” Scientists use light to measure the vast distances of space. Light travels at about 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) a second in a vacuum. A ray of sunlight passing Earth takes about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon, about four hours to reach Neptune, and another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1. For comparison, a light-year is 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers). Even though the team has not received science and engineering data from Voyager 1 since Nov. 14, the spacecraft is sending what is called a carrier signal, which typically conveys that data to Earth. Mission engineers used the carrier signal and trajectory calculations to confirm the light-day milestone. They continue to analyze the issue impacting the science and engineering data. Humanity’s only probes in interstellar space, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, launched in 1977 to take advantage of a rare planetary alignment. Managed by JPL, they were only the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn, and the first to return high-resolution imagery, transforming our understanding of these worlds and their moons. Voyager 2 went on to study the ethereal ice giants, Neptune and Uranus. Both spacecraft continue to measure changes in the Sun’s magnetic field across vast distances. “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.” In addition to their suite of scientific instruments, the Voyager probes carry a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph compiling images and sounds from Earth, as a message to any advanced civilization that might one day find it. “Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.” Launched in 1977, Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, transformed our understanding of the solar system through their exploration of the outer planets. In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first human-made spacecraft to enter interstellar space. On Nov. 18, 2026, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth. Milestones, challenges Traveling about 38,000 mph (61,155 kph), Voyager 1 in 2012 became the first spacecraft to leave the heliosphere, the bubble of particles and magnetic fields created by the Sun that deflects cosmic radiation, and enter interstellar space. Voyager 2, taking a different trajectory, crossed the boundary in 2018. “The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.” Creative engineering solutions have enabled the probes to conserve energy and overcome challenges related to aging hardware, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer on the spacecraft. Earlier this year, engineers successfully turned off three devices on Voyager 1 and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives — a move not without risk — to help the spacecraft make the most of its 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator. Essentially a nuclear battery, the generator converts heat from decaying plutonium into electricity. With the plutonium supply continually depleting, both Voyager probes lose about 4 watts of power each year. The latest energy-saving effort is expected to provide enough power for both spacecraft to keep their current suite of science instruments operating until at least their 50th launch anniversaries next summer. As with all NASA spacecraft that venture to and beyond the Moon, communication between Earth and the Voyager probes is managed by the agency’s Deep Space Network, large antennas located at three facilities around the world. “We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.” For more information about NASA’s Voyager mission, visit: https://science. Nasa. Gov/mission/voyager/ -end- Abbey Interrante / Karen Fox Headquarters, Washington 202-358-1600 abbey. A. Interrante@nasa. Gov / karen. C. Fox@nasa. summary: Voyager 1, depicted in this artist’s concept, reached one light-day from Earth on Nov. 18, 2026.
author: NASA News

title: NASA hot‑fire tests RS‑25 engine No. 10001 at Stennis, supporting Artemis missions
content:
NASA performed a hot‑fire test of RS‑25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at the Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Nov. 18, 2026. The developmental engine was fired for the planned 200 seconds—three minutes and twenty seconds—by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris Technologies, and Nova Space Solutions.

Although this particular RS‑25 will not fly, the test is intended to capture critical data that can be used to improve engine performance and reliability for future Artemis missions. For each Artemis launch, four RS‑25 engines generate up to two million pounds of combined thrust to propel the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket.

The upcoming Artemis IV mission, slated for 2028, will launch astronauts aboard the Orion spacecraft from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. That mission is described as a key step toward exploring the lunar South Pole, establishing an enduring human presence on the Moon, and building a foundation for the first crewed mission to Mars.

All RS‑25 engines undergo testing and are proven flight‑worthy at NASA’s Stennis facility before being used on SLS flights. The November test adds to the data set supporting the agency’s broader lunar exploration goals.
summary: 1 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA conducts a hot fire test of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St.
author: NASA News

title: Astronaut photographs Lake Pelku from the International Space Station
content:
An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed Lake Pelku, visible near the center of the image, while the station passed over Asia. The photograph was taken by Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and is credited to CSA/Joshua Kutryk.

The International Space Station is described as a unique platform for Earth observation, employing both hands‑on and automated equipment. Station crew members have generated hundreds of thousands of images that record real‑time phenomena and aid research and disaster‑relief efforts.
summary: An astronaut on the International Space Station captured a photograph of Lake Pelku near the center of the image while the station orbited above Asia. title: New cryptography-based method finds pulsar PSR J1622−7204 1 million times faster
content:
An international research team has unveiled a new computational method that can locate pulsars in NASA’s publicly available Fermi Gamma‑ray Space Telescope data up to a million times faster than previous techniques. The breakthrough, described in a paper published Thursday in Physical Review Letters, was achieved by applying a cryptography‑inspired lattice algorithm to 15 years of gamma‑ray observations from the Fermi telescope.

Using the new approach, the scientists identified PSR J1622−7204, an isolated pulsar that spins 261 times per second. The detection required only the equivalent of ten hours of processing on a standard computer processor, whereas the best earlier method would have needed a processor to run for roughly 600 years to achieve the same result. The algorithm, developed by Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay of the Weizmann Institute of Science, reformulates the pulsar search as a problem of finding the shortest vector in a high‑dimensional lattice—a technique originally created for breaking encryption systems.

Lead author Daniel Pook‑Kolb, a scientist at the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics (Albert Einstein Institute), explained that traditional searches must explore a four‑dimensional parameter space—spin rate, spin‑down rate, sky position, and another variable—requiring an impractically large number of calculations. By converting the search into a geometry problem, each trial of the new algorithm runs in about five minutes on a single laptop core, making the process feasible on ordinary hardware.

The team plans to extend the method to locate pulsars in binary systems, where a companion star’s gravity distorts the pulsar signal and has previously rendered such searches ineffective. Colin Clark, an astrophysicist at the Max Planck Institute and co‑author of the study, noted that tens or even hundreds of similar pulsars may already be hidden in the existing data set. He added that the next phase will combine the lattice algorithm with the crowdsourced computing power of the Einstein@Home volunteer network.

The discovery underscores the impact of NASA’s open‑data policy. Since its launch in 2008, the Fermi telescope has scanned the entire sky every three hours, and after an initial calibration period all data have been released publicly and continue to be updated. Open software tools such as NASA’s Fermitools enabled the researchers to prepare the dataset for analysis, and the accessibility of the archive allows any team to replicate or build upon the work, a point emphasized by Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center.
summary: 5 min read NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars NASA’s Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, illustrated here, scans the entire sky every three hours as it orbits Earth. Its publicly available data helps scientists find the rapidly spinning cores of dead stars, known as pulsars.

title: NASA TTT launches public challenge on life in 2075 with $20,000 prizes
content:
